boeing.public_statement:
Back in 2025 I said we were turning the ship but hadn't turned it. I think we've turned it now. The balance sheet is repaired and staying repaired. The 737 line has built at 57 a month to plan for five straight years. The 777X and the MAX family are delivering. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here, and the job now is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. We'll do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. We've looked hard at it with the data in front of us, and the case isn't there yet. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we do go, we build it at rate the right way. With new engines in development at Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and CFM always at the table, we expect to give our customers a choice of engine, with durability proven before entry into service. When we launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year either. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

On production, the 737 stays at 57 a month and stays stable. Any step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We're keeping our trained people and our suppliers ready. Going slow has let us go faster, and stability is what lets us move when the time comes.

Our dates will be set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see. This is the frame's lean, confirmed by both memos.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. Pope's KPI gate is clean and her veto is not invoked. No Rate Increase is on the menu. CFM's sub-tier shortages are a watch item, not a live problem.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1303]
   - Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress on every 10-year row.
   - Technology: ready by EIS. GTF2 is ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037, CFM always.
   - Market: not ready on this grid. No fps row beats Do Nothing in any column.
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's slip leg, S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01, line -3.01):
   - Pass: Do Nothing, the Re-engine and the four 10-year rows.
   - Fail (binding): every 7-year and via-Embraer row.
   This round S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so the leg works as a level test.
   Pope's priors are unpriced but point the same way: a clean-sheet +3 years puts a 10-year fps at 2048; a derivative +2 years puts the Re-engine at 2042.
4. Is this doing less, better? [BX-1239] Yes. Do Nothing beats every fps row by $1.20B or more in every column. The only plans within ε of it in S1 (10-year + Re-engine rows) have worst columns $3.51-3.88B lower.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding buffer veto strikes every 7-year and via-Embraer row. None was ordered.
- Pope's H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is honoured: not ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto: no object this round.
- I decided the rest. No overrides.

fps: HOLD
- The best row, 10-year at Renton, gives up $1.20 / $1.46 / $1.20 / $1.22B (S1 to S4).
- My debt-first test needs a plan more than ε ahead of Do Nothing in S1. It is $2.20B short. The Board's -$1B per-item line fails in every column.
- An objective premium of $1.20B (S1) would sit inside my $2B cap. I won't use it: it would carry an item that fails my own test and the Board's line. 50/50 is the company's mission, not on my ranked list.
- Pope's discounting check shows the narrowing from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20 is mostly five years of discounting (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26). The case has moved later; it has not got better.
- Cost of waiting, said plainly. There is no 2040 round, so the earliest fps EIS becomes 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year). Under the lead-edge rule the long-run share falls from 42-45% (a 2035 launch) to 32-35% (a 2045 launch).
- The grid assumes nobody moves later, so it cannot price a 2045 launch. Malave confirms nothing in the brief puts a dollar figure on it. It is information for the 2045 case, not a reason to launch now. Airbus's 2037 date does not set ours [B-2313, B-2315].
- Ramp and route for 2045: the 10-year ramp, Solo. The 7-year fails the buffer and stress debt at new sites. Via Embraer sits $10.95-11.47B behind Solo with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty, and Pope finds it adds no IP or capacity.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call)
- Item value: +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4; -1.63 in S3. It passes Malave's buffer by $2.01B and debt holds at $0. In my expected column it is the best plan.
- Three grounds move me to hold:
  (a) The Board will veto it under its -$1B per-item line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine: Airbus says 'A350 family', and RR is waiting with a widebody UltraFan for 'a Re-engine on the table'. I have no override against the Board. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
  (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], has updated his read on the evidence: from 40-50% to about 30% (25-35%). That puts the weighted edge at +$0.92B ($0.74-1.10B). At the centre that is inside ε, so the higher worst column decides: Do Nothing -2.47 against -4.10. He also notes the +2.01 is a ceiling: it assumes Airbus never re-engines later.
  (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low. A launch now is a one-way door, since the EIS is 2040 and there is no round before it (H5).
- I'm not hiding what the hold costs. Pope shows 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay takes about 9.5% off its value. A 2045 Re-engine would meet a 2045 fps at H4's limit, so this hold may in practice close the programme.
- The cost is logged separately, as a Board-downside hold and not against the cap: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4; $1.63B saved in S3; $0.92B weighted at 30%.
- My reading of Airbus's probability is Low confidence on my record. I relied on Malave's read and on company doctrine (profile §7, the A330neo precedent [B-2446]).

SITE, CODE, RATE
- fps_site: new_site. Renton is worth 0.00 without a launch, and the full $3.0B capex saving needs only a choice 3 years before EIS.
- Engine code: null with the hold. At launch it will be code 7: three sources, all ready by EIS, an allowed pair against NGSA. That is doctrine and my public requirement; I have no record as Boeing CEO on engine choice.
- rate_737: hold, the only value. The ceiling stays at 57.

HARD RULES AND RED LINES
- H1: the 2030 ruling stands and is not re-made.
- H3, first half: lifted in 2030. Second half: in force. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the 787 Re-engine stays open but is held.
- H4: respected, with no development in flight.
- H5: nothing to cancel.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: soft total $0.
- H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- My own red lines are all respected: no concurrency, no fixed-price development, no FAA blame, no attribution of supplier problems to Airbus.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): -1.01 / -0.02 / -2.47 / -1.01.
- No Board items: fps, re787 and fps_site are each at their default, so every item value is 0.00.
- Expected column: S1. Risk case S4 is -1.01: 0.00 against Do Nothing, with $2.00B of headroom over -3.01. Buffer: pass.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547], and net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060. The grid holds the fps back, not the cash.
- Pope's gates: KPI clean; zero strain; engines ready by any EIS; no concurrency; Renton not chosen, with a bridge plan drafted for 2045.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine is logged as a Board-downside hold.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- the A350 probability (via Malave);
- engine code 7;
- the Renton bridge plan;
- the slip priors.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input on the Re-engine, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer: accepted to the cent. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows are struck. The 10-year rows pass, but at new sites with only $0.39B of headroom.
- Net debt: accepted from the metrics table. The debt penalty is already netted and not subtracted again.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass, accepted.
- Cash timing: accepted. The 10-year peaks at $8.44B in 2041, 92% of stress free cash flow. In cash, a same-round Re-engine falls entirely inside the fps spend.
- What moved me: his updated A350 read of about 30%, which he moved down on two of his own 2030 triggers. It puts the weighted edge just inside ε, so the higher worst column decides. That supports the Board's line rather than standing in for it.
- I log his offer: he would support the Re-engine on evidence that puts the A350 chance below 28%. That is the trigger to carry forward.
- His point that +2.01 is an undiscounted ceiling (it assumes no later A350 move) is noted.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I took her memo as gates and facts, not judgement.
- Accepted: the KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object; the 737 ceiling stays at 57. Strain is zero on the hold; a 2035 10-year + Re-engine pair sits at H4's limit, and a 7-year pair breaches it. Engines for code 7 are ready 5-9 years before EIS. Via Embraer fails the partner test. Re-engine readiness passes on the GEnx upgrade.
- Two of her findings sharpened the rationale. Her discounting check (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26) shows the fps case has moved later, not improved. And 2035 is the only zero-strain Re-engine slot against a 2045 fps, so I've said plainly that the hold may close it.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan and her 2045 readiness plan (workforce through the dip, fragile suppliers, production system proven at rate, one KPI-gated ask at a time) go into the other moves.
- Her statement that operations does not hold the Re-engine back is accepted. The hold rests on the market column S3 and the Board's line, not on readiness.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1: rivals hold. Airbus keeps its Alt plan; per the bulletin it reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event, and none is on the record. No A350 Re-engine.
- S2 (Airbus back on its base plan) is the upside.
- S3 (an A350 Re-engine, about 30% on Malave's read) is the plausible downside.
- S4 (Delay Tactics) is the risk case. It equals S1 on every hold row.
The column values our plan; it does not set our dates [B-2313].
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (+1.00). I chose fps: hold + 787: hold (-1.01), $2.01B below it. That is a Board-downside hold: the Board's -$1B per-item line binds while S3 (-1.63) is not ruled out, and I have no override. It is logged separately and not against the cap. Weighted at Malave's 30% read of an A350 Re-engine, the gap is $0.92B, inside ε, where the higher worst column (-2.47 against -4.10) decides.
boeing.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0. Objective premium: $0.
- fps hold: no premium, because the grid prefers it. The best fps row (10-year at Renton) sits $1.20B below Do Nothing in S1 and $1.46B below in S2. Launching it for 50/50, incumbency or the engine enabler would be an objective premium of $1.20B. That is inside the cap, but it fails my debt-first test and the Board's -$1B line, so it is not taken.
- 787 Re-engine hold: a known cost, logged separately as a Board-downside hold, as the Board asked. It gives up $2.01B in S1, S2 and S4 and saves $1.63B in S3. Weighted at Malave's 30% (25-35%), the cost is $0.92B ($0.74-1.10B).
- What breaks the number: if the A350 does not re-engine, the hold gives up the full $2.01B. If it does, the hold saves $1.63B, and H3 closes the 787 Re-engine for good.
boeing.objective_note:
The objectives never change the payoff.
- Hold the 50/50 split: unmet on every hold plan. Preference share falls to 37% at NGSA's 2037 EIS and 20% from 2043. Not chased: the premium needed would breach the Board's line and my own debt-first test.
- Defend incumbency: unmet (worst year 20%). Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45 and recovers to 36.3% from 2047, when Airbus's capacity binds. This is the long-cycle stake the 2045 fps case must answer. Waiting costs share: 42-45% for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch. The grid does not price it.
- Balance sheet, repair and keep repaired (base and stress): met. Net debt is $0 from 2029 through 2050.
- Engine enabler, three makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, RR).
- Engine enabler, two or three sources on our narrowbody: unmet, since the MAX flies CFM only. It is answered at launch by code 7 and by the public, dateless engine-sourcing requirement.
boeing.predictions:
AIRBUS
- NGSA enters service in 2037 on schedule, and Airbus keeps the Alt plan (S1).
- An A350 Re-engine this round is about 30% (Malave's read). Airbus's engineering is on NGSA first, but its 'A350 family' wording and RR's waiting widebody UltraFan keep it open.
- No Delay Tactics effect: with no fps they would be 'naked' and draw a $48.32B fine, and S4 equals S1 on our hold.

ENGINE MAKERS
- GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both fitted to NGSA.
- CFM keeps the LEAP-1B on the MAX.
- No widebody UltraFan, since no Re-engine is on the table.

OUR RESULTS IF NOBODY MOVES AGAIN
- ΔPV: -1.01 (S1), -0.02 (S2), -2.47 (S3), -1.01 (S4).
- Net debt $0 in base and stress at every check year.
- NB preference share 37% in 2037 and 20% from 2043.
- MAX deliveries 409-468 a year in 2038-42, back to 684 from 2047.
- WB share 58.8%.

2045
- Bring the staged fps case: Solo, the 10-year ramp, Renton with a bridge plan, code 7, against the Board's two lines and Malave's slip leg.
- Re-test the 787 Re-engine only if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced under H4.

board_response.recommendation: Hold the fps with no date; keep the staged 2045 case (authority to offer first) with the 10-year ramp, Renton with a MAX bridge plan, item values against both lines, and the cost of waiting under the lead-edge rule set out as information.
board_response.response: Taken. fps: hold, new_site, no date in the public statement. The staged 2045 case is a private other move: Solo, the 10-year ramp, Renton only with Pope's five-step bridge plan, code 7, item values in every column against your -$1B and +$1B lines, and Malave's slip leg as the baseline. The cost of waiting is set out: 42-45% long-run for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch, unpriced on this grid. It is information for 2045, not a reason to launch. I also note Pope's finding that the narrowing from -2.08 to -1.20 is mostly discounting.

board_response.recommendation: Log any objective premium against the $2B cap; the -$1B per-item line binds first; answer the long-cycle stake with a case that clears the tests.
board_response.response: Taken. Objective premium $0, soft premium $0. Launching the 10-year at Renton would have needed $1.20B (S1) to $1.46B (S2). I did not bring it, because it fails your line and my own debt-first test. The long-cycle stake (preference share at 20% from 2043) is acknowledged in the objective note and will be answered by the 2045 case, not by a premium now.

board_response.recommendation: Hold the 787 Re-engine as a Board-downside hold, logged separately; re-test in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced under H4.
board_response.response: Taken: re787 hold. Logged separately, not against the cap: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4, $1.63B saved in S3, and $0.92B weighted at Malave's updated 30% read. Re-test it in 2045 only if H3's second half has not closed it. Plainly: Pope shows 2035 is the only zero-strain slot against a 2045 fps, so a 2045 Re-engine would meet that fps at H4's 2-year limit (10-year) or breach it (7-year).

board_response.recommendation: Show the submitted plan's S4 against Do Nothing with Malave's buffer number, his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result and the base and stress net-debt line; do not subtract the debt penalty again.
board_response.response: Taken. The submitted plan is Do Nothing: S4 -1.01, 0.00 against Do Nothing, $2.00B of headroom over -3.01, a buffer pass. Fundable when the 777X turns: pass (777X cash-positive since 2029, net debt $0). Net debt: '2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B)' in every column, base and stress, to 2060. The debt penalty is not subtracted again.

board_response.recommendation: Pope's memo states the KPI gate, engineering capacity, supplier readiness and two-front strain; MAX bridge plan and no concurrency if Renton.
Keep the engine-sourcing requirement dateless with durability before EIS; at launch name a code whose makers are ready by EIS (code 7 on the record).
board_response.response: Taken. The public engine-sourcing requirement is updated and still dateless: all three makers are invited, selection is among launched engines, and durability proven before EIS is a contract condition. With GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) in development, the plan at launch is code 7, an allowed pair against NGSA. The engine code is null with the hold.

board_response.recommendation: Surplus cash is reserved to the Board; keep headroom for the staged fps; no dividend or buyback signal.
board_response.response: Taken. The public statement makes no dividend or buyback signal. Surplus allocation is left to the Board (a private other move). The headroom flagged is $60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year (61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow).

board_response.recommendation: Do not let Airbus set our dates; neither a launch nor a hold cites NGSA's EIS, the Alt-plan gate or any A350 move as its reason.
board_response.response: Taken. The fps hold rests on our own grid: no row beats Do Nothing, and the debt-first test fails. The public statement says our dates are set by our own readiness. The Re-engine hold rests on your downside line and on the market column S3, read from the bulletin, not on Airbus's timing. The expected column values the plan; it does not set our dates.

priorities: Safety and production readiness first. We approve no launch without Pope's KPI, engineering-capacity, supplier and strain results. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, and the 737 holds at 57 a month. Her memo must still say so. If Renton is proposed, it must come with a MAX bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069].

Proof before commitment on the fps: one well-founded launch, not a bet. This grid still gives no fps launch a business case. The best is launch_10yr at Renton with re787 hold. Its item value is -1.20 / -1.46 / -1.20 / -1.22 (S1-S4): $0.20B short of our -$1B line in its best column, and at least $2.20B short of the +$1B business-case line. Malave's buffer no longer stands against the 10-year ramp (S4 -2.23 against a line of -3.01), but our own tests do [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581, BG-0068, B-2303].

The balance sheet stays repaired. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Any plan must sit within $2B of Do Nothing in the risk-case column S4 (Do Nothing -1.01, line -3.01). The 10-year rows pass this test. Every 7-year and via-Embraer row fails it. Surplus cash is a matter reserved to the Board [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BG-0034, B-2259].

One development at a time, and the 787 Re-engine on its downside. On its own it is worth +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4 but -1.63 in S3, an A350 Re-engine that the bulletin does not rule out. It breaches our -$1B line again, so it waits, logged as a Board-downside hold. With a 7-year fps it would also overlap by 5 years [BG-0066, B-2167, BG-0022].

Decide on Boeing's own case, never as a reply to Airbus. NGSA's 2037 EIS and Airbus's Alt-plan gate do not set our dates. Between the ramps our rule picks the 10-year: it is better by $2.48-2.75B in every column and has the higher worst column (-3.67 against -6.15 at Renton) [B-2313, B-2315, BG-0068].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged since 2030. No Board item may lose more than $1B against its default in any plausible column, and all four columns count: the bulletin rules out no A350 Re-engine, and Delay Tactics are covert. The plan must sit within $2B of Do Nothing in the risk case S4 (line -3.01). At horizon 3 the fps gets no extra downside allowance for its long-term position. The balance sheet is repaired on the brief, so this round the binding limit is the per-item downside line, not the rating.
board_guidance.expect_to_see: (1) The submitted row. For each Board item, the same row with that field at its default (fps hold, re787 hold, fps_site new_site), and the item value in S1-S4. (2) The CEO's expected column, justified from the bulletin, and the risk-case column S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01; the line is -3.01). (3) Malave's buffer test with the numbers, his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result, and the net-debt line in base and stress from the brief's metrics table. (4) Pope's KPI, engineering, supplier and two-front-strain results. These include the H4 overlap of any fps and Re-engine pair (a 2-year limit), no production-certification concurrency, and a MAX bridge plan if fps_site is renton. (5) Confirmation that H3's second half is still in force (no 787 Re-engine once the A350 Re-engine has launched). The Round-1 H1 ruling is not needed again. (6) Every soft doctrine or objective premium in $B, with its reason, set against the $2B cap. The known cost of any Board-downside hold (the Re-engine) is to be stated separately. (7) For any fps launch, the engine code, with each named maker's engine ready by EIS. (8) A board_response to each recommendation below.
would_approve: fps: hold (Do Nothing). This is not a Board item and is never vetoed. Do Nothing scores -1.01 / -0.02 / -2.47 / -1.01, with net debt at $0 in base and stress in every column.
re787: hold (the default).

recommendations.text: Hold the fps this round and give no fps date in the public statement. frame.situation:
Round 2, decision year 2035. We launched nothing in 2030. We are on today's products: the 737 MAX at 57 a month (684 a year) and the 787.

**Public record**
- Airbus launched NGSA in 2030 for an EIS in 2037, with engine code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR).
- Airbus is on its Alt plan: A320 lines kept longer through the NGSA ramp. The plan is re-checked at the 2035 gate and reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. None of the three is on the record.
- P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037) launched on NGSA's selection. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- No A350 Re-engine has been launched, so H3's second half has not closed the 787 Re-engine.
- Airbus says its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. Both are signals, not a rule-out.

**Market on Do Nothing**
- Delivered share was 40.1% in 2030-34. Our firm backlog was all delivered by 2033. The waiting backlog falls from 1,319 (2033) to 763 (2035) and reaches zero by 2038.
- From NGSA's EIS, our preference share falls 3 pp a year: 37% in 2037, and 20% from 2043.
- Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45. It recovers to 36.3% from 2047, because Airbus's capacity of about 1,200 a year binds and its flexible customers take our free slots.
- That is why Do Nothing loses only $1.01B in S1: narrowbody operating profit is -3.64, offset by +2.63 from supply and demand.

**Balance sheet**
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and stays there to 2060 in both base and stress.
- Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. On Do Nothing, profit runs $0.13-0.78B a year below the game baseline in 2037-45.
- How the surplus is used is the Board's decision.

**Objectives**
- Balance-sheet lines: all met.
- 50/50 split and incumbency: not met (worst year 20%).
- Engine enabler: three narrowbody makers in the market in 2045 and 2050 is met. Two or three sources on our own narrowbody is not met (the MAX flies CFM only). Every 10-year Solo row shows 3 sources in 2050.

**KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The MAX delivered to plan. The Rate Increase is not on the menu (it was a 2030-only order).

**Item values against Do Nothing (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)**
- 787 Re-engine alone: +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01. In 2030 it was +3.30 / -2.48, so its edge is narrowing.
- fps 10-year at Renton: -1.20 / -1.46 / -1.20 / -1.22. At new sites: -1.58 / -1.82 / -1.58 / -1.61.
- fps 7-year: -3.68 to -4.48.
- fps via Embraer, hold rows: -12.16 to -12.78.
- Renton adds +0.36 to +0.39 on the 10-year ramp and +0.42 to +0.58 on the 7-year, and only alongside a launch.
- Best plan by column: the Re-engine alone in S1, S2 and S4 (+1.00, +1.99, +1.00); Do Nothing in S3 (-2.47).

**Board guidance.** It does not bind, but its veto binds after my decision.
- It would veto every fps launch. The 10-year fails its -$1B per-item line in every column and its +$1B business-case test. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows also fail Malave's buffer.
- It would veto the 787 Re-engine: S3 at -1.63 breaks its -$1B line, and the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine.
- It would approve a hold on both, and new_site. It would take Renton only with a launch it approves and a MAX bridge plan, and it wants code 7 at any launch.
- It wants to see:
  - S4 against Do Nothing;
  - Malave's buffer and 'Fundable when the 777X turns' results;
  - net debt in base and stress;
  - Pope's gates;
  - H3's second half confirmed;
  - every premium logged;
  - the cost of waiting set out for 2045.

These are Board risks for our package, not red lines.

None is on the record, and GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) are on schedule. Choosing S1 or S2 changes no ranking, because the Re-engine is +2.01 in both. Two plans sit within ε of Do Nothing in S1:

- 10-yr + Re-engine: -1.25 (-0.24); worst column -6.35.
Do Nothing's worst column is -2.47, so Do Nothing wins.

Worst columns against Do Nothing's -2.47 (S3):
- Re-engine: -4.10 (-1.63).
- 10-yr at Renton: -3.67 (-1.20).
- 10-yr at new site: -4.05 (-1.58).
- 10-yr at Renton + Re-engine: -5.98 (-3.51).

tests.name: Meet and beat: 787 Re-engine at my updated A350 read (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: I back the launch only if its edge over Do Nothing, weighted at p, exceeds ε: 2.01 - 3.64p > 1.01, so p < 27.7%. The edge is zero at p = 55.2%. Your thresholds are confirmed.
tests.numbers:
Item value: +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01.

My updated p, the chance of an A350 Re-engine this round, is about 30% (range 25-35%). It was 40-50% in 2030, from doctrine, not my record.

What moves it down:
- Two of the three signals I named in 2030 are now on the record. NGSA is in development to 2037 with first claim on Airbus resources (the Alt-plan text), and Airbus keeps its widebody focus on the A350 family and the A350F.
- The early A350 move that doctrine expected did not come in 2030.

What holds it up:
- RR is waiting, not walking away. 'No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table' keeps an engine ready to answer one.
- 'A350 family' does not exclude a re-engined A350.
- The A330neo precedent says Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446].
Nothing rules S3 out, so the Board's -$1B line binds.

Edge: +1.10 at 25%, +0.92 at 30%, +0.74 at 35%. My central read is $0.08B inside ε, so the higher worst column decides: Do Nothing -2.47 over -4.10.

What breaks the +2.01: the grid assumes nobody moves later. An A350 Re-engine in any later round would also cut the re-engined 787's margin to 15.77% and stop its share gains (dashboard_game §2). So +2.01 is a ceiling the grid does not discount.

The Re-engine passes my buffer. This is advice, not a veto.

tests.name: Balance sheet first: net debt in base and stress (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: The grid already nets the debt penalty (α 0.30, debt × α × (debt ÷ EV)²), so it is never subtracted again. Net debt must be at or below $0 at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, in base and stress (brief metrics table). Between plans within ε on the expected column, prefer the one with the smaller added penalty (inference).
tests.numbers:
Confirmed from the metrics table. Do Nothing, the Re-engine and all four 10-yr rows read '2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B)' in every column. Base holds ('yes') on every row of the grid.

Stress fails on:
- 7-yr at new site: all four columns (peaks $0.8B, $0.6B, $0.8B, $0.8B).
- 7-yr + Re-engine: all four ($3.0B, $2.7B, $3.5B, $3.0B).

Undiscounted penalties, for scale only (each move alone, not additive): 10-yr fps $19.1B, 7-yr $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B.

Within ε in S1, Do Nothing (no added penalty) beats both 10-yr + Re-engine rows. At my central A350 read, it beats the Re-engine ($0.6B penalty) on the same ground.

tests.name: Fundable when the 777X turns (CEO ask 5; a Board gate)
tests.threshold: The fps is fundable once the 777X is cash-positive (from 2029) and the balance sheet is repaired. A launch passes unless the brief shows otherwise (inference).
tests.numbers:

The brief shows otherwise only for the 7-yr new-site rows, the 7-yr + Re-engine rows and most via-Embraer cells. The gate is met: the grid holds the fps back, not the cash.

tests.name: Cash path of each bill (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: When each bill lands (the board books it at EIS; the tracker spends it over development on the standard curve), and whether two land together
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan: no bill and no programme cash.

Each bill:
- 10-yr fps: $60.32B over 2035-45. Year 1 at 5% is $3.02B. The peak at 14% is $8.44B in year 7 (2041): 61% of base free cash flow ($13.8B) and 92% of stress free cash flow ($9.2B). Booked at EIS 2045.
- 7-yr fps: $65.00B over 2035-42, $9.29B a year on average: 67% of base and 101% of stress free cash flow, which is why stress fails at new sites. Booked 2042.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, about $1.0B a year. Booked 2040.

On the board's booking, no two bills land in the same year (2040, 2042, 2045). In cash, a same-round pair does run together: the Re-engine's whole $5B falls inside the fps spend.
- With the 10-yr, the strain overlap is 2038-40: $1.2B undiscounted, at H4's limit with no slack. Net debt still holds at $0 in stress.
- With the 7-yr, it is 2035-40: $3.0B, an H4 breach. Stress fails.

Renton's ~$3.0B capex saving is full if Renton is chosen by 2042 for a 2045 EIS, so keeping new_site with a hold loses nothing.

Sequencing: a 2035 Re-engine (2035-40) clears any 2045 fps strain window (10-yr 2048-55, 7-yr 2045-52). A 2045 Re-engine beside a 2045 fps would overlap by 2 years (10-yr) or 5 (7-yr).

tests.name: Cost of waiting: fps and 787 Re-engine (CEO asks 2 and 7)
tests.threshold: Price waiting only where the brief gives a dollar figure; otherwise it is information for 2045 (inference)
tests.numbers:
fps: nothing in the brief prices a 2045 launch, because the grid assumes nobody moves after this round.
- The long-run splits (42% or 45% for a 2035 launch, 32% or 35% for a 2045 launch) are preference shares under the public lead-edge rule. They are objective lines, not dollars.
- On this board, Do Nothing's loss is in share, not lasting profit. Profit runs $0.13-0.78B a year below the game baseline in 2037-45. It is back at the status-quo $6.2B from 2047, when Airbus's ~1,200 cap returns our slots (delivered share 36.3%).
- The one dollar trend on the record runs against haste: the best fps item went from -2.08 (2030 grid) to -1.20 now.
Agreed: this is information for 2045, not a reason to launch.

Re-engine:
- In five years its edge fell from +3.30 to +2.01 (-$1.29B), while its downside narrowed from -2.48 to -1.63 (+$0.85B). The ε threshold moved from 39.8% to 27.7%.
- A 2045 launch enters service in 2050. The grid does not price it, H3 closes it for good if the A350 moves first, and it would meet a 2045 fps under H4.
- No round falls between 2035 and the Re-engine's 2040 EIS, so a launch now is a one-way door (H5).

tests.name: Full cost of a slip or cancel
tests.threshold: Cancel write-off = bill × years elapsed ÷ development years, and the debt penalty stays; cost it once, in full. H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine.
tests.numbers: Nothing is launched, so nothing can be cancelled. Any 2035 launch is in effect irreversible: the Re-engine (EIS 2040) and a 7-yr fps (EIS 2042) enter service before the next round. A 10-yr fps would be at its EIS by 2045, with its full $60.32B spent and its penalty staying. We launch only what we will finish (H5).

tests.name: Rate step
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA. Never as a reply to Airbus, and never under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem (H6).
tests.numbers: rate_737 is hold only: the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the MAX delivers to plan at 57 a month (684 a year). The KPI gate is Pope's to state.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Every doctrine or objective premium is reported in $B, with the soft total at most $2B. Board-downside holds are logged separately. Name the condition that would break the number.
tests.numbers:
Expected column: S1.
- fps hold: no premium. The grid prefers hold; the best fps row (10-yr at Renton) is $1.20B below in S1 and $1.46B below in S2.
- Objective premium: $0, since nothing is chased. Launching the 10-yr at Renton anyway would be an objective premium of $1.20B (S1) or $1.46B (S2). That is inside the $2B cap, but it fails the Board's -$1B line and your debt-first test, so I do not recommend it.
- Re-engine hold: a Board-downside hold, logged separately and not against the cap. Known cost: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4, and $1.63B saved in S3. Weighted at my read of about 30% (25-35%), it costs $0.92B ($0.74-1.10B). It is not a soft premium: the binding reason is the Board's line, and its full-column cost is $0.01B above the cap in any case.
- Soft total against the cap: $0 of $2B.

Conditions that break the numbers:
- Do Nothing's -1.01 (S1) holds barring an A350 Re-engine this round; with one, it becomes -2.47.
- The Re-engine hold gives up the full $2.01B barring an A350 move.

vetoes.plan: All four fps launch_7yr rows (new site or Renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine)

Buffer test (slip leg), risk-case column S4 against Do Nothing's -1.01; the line is -3.01.

vetoes.plan: All four fps launch_via_embraer rows

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (alone)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, NOT a veto. It passes my buffer: S4 is +1.00, 2.01 above Do Nothing. Net debt holds at $0 in base and stress.

Its worst column is S3, 1.63 below Do Nothing (-4.10 against -2.47). At my updated A350 read of about 30% (25-35%), its edge is +$0.92B (+0.74 to +1.10), inside ε at the centre, so the higher worst column decides for hold. The +2.01 also assumes Airbus never re-engines later.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_10yr rows (new site or Renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, NOT a veto. All four pass my buffer, with S4 headroom of 0.39 (new site), 0.78 (Renton), 1.73 (+ Re-engine) and 2.11 (Renton + Re-engine).

Alone they are 1.20-1.82 below Do Nothing in every column. With the Re-engine they are 1.88-2.50 below the Re-engine alone, and the 2-year strain overlap ($1.2B) sits at H4's limit with no slack. The new-site row has only $0.39B of headroom.

Hold. If the fps is ever launched, use code 7: GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) are ready by EIS. This is doctrine and our public requirement, not my record.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
787 Re-engine: I would back re787: launch if the public record gives me grounds to put the chance of an A350 Re-engine this round below about 28%, so that its edge (2.01 - 3.64p) clears ε. Examples:
- Airbus commits its widebody engineering to the A350F and NGSA with no new engine;
- RR turns to a Trent upgrade rather than holding UltraFan WB for a re-engine;
- the Board accepts that S3 is not plausible, or relaxes its -$1B per-item line for a derivative carrying a $0.6B penalty.
It already clears my buffer by $2.01B, and a 2035 start clears any 2045 fps window, so in that case I would support it, not merely concur. An A350 Re-engine on the record closes it for good (H3).

fps: I would back a launch on any row that sits within $2B of Do Nothing in S4 and more than ε above it in the expected column. There is none on this grid. In 2045 I would take whichever ramp passes the slip leg with the higher worst column.

Balance sheet: if the chosen row's stress-case net debt rose above $0, I would hold whatever drives it.

A live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem would only confirm hold.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the buffer as the baseline: S4 no worse than -3.01, $2B under Do Nothing's -1.01. Your list is right. Every 7-year and via-Embraer row fails, $1.01B to $10.57B past the line, and that veto binds. One note: S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so this round the slip leg is really a level test.

fps: the 10-year rows clear my buffer, but none beats Do Nothing in any column; the best, at Renton, gives up $1.20-1.46B. It is fundable: the 777X turned in 2029 and net debt holds at zero in base and stress. The grid holds it back, not the cash. Nothing in the brief prices a 2045 launch, and the one dollar trend on record runs the other way: -2.08 in 2030, -1.20 now.

787 Re-engine: it clears my buffer by $2.01B and debt stays at zero, so no veto. The signals I named in 2030 have partly come in: Airbus's engineering goes to NGSA first, its widebody focus to the A350 and A350F. RR is waiting, not walking away, and nothing rules S3 out. My read moves from 40-50% to about 30%. That puts the edge at +$0.92B, just inside ε, where I take the higher worst column: -2.47 over -4.10. And the +2.01 holds only barring a later A350 Re-engine too.

So, Do Nothing: a higher confidence plan. Log the Re-engine as a Board-downside hold: $2.01B given up, $1.63B saved in S3. We're bullish on 2045.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S4 (Airbus Delay Tactics) against the nominal S1 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. The doctrine slip priors are not priced on the board.
tests.numbers: MAX: 684 a year (57 a month) delivered exactly to the public plan in 2030-34. Risk case S4 against S1: Do Nothing -1.01 / -1.01 and the Re-engine alone +1.00 / +1.00. 100% of their value survives Delay Tactics, which act only from fps EIS. The fps rows lose little to S4: 10-year 0.02-0.03, 7-year 0.10-0.26, via Embraer 0.02-0.03. The board prices no slip. Sensitivity (inference: discounting at the 10.5% WACC only, with no cost overrun): each year of later EIS takes about 9.5% off a programme's value. The Re-engine's fall from +3.30 (2030 grid, EIS 2035) to +2.01 (EIS 2040) is five years of discounting: 3.30 / 1.105^5 = 2.00. On the derivative slip prior (+2 years, range +1 to +4; doctrine), a 2035 Re-engine loses about $0.36B (to +1.65), or $0.66B at +4 years (to +1.35). It stays positive in S1, S2 and S4. fps, on the clean-sheet prior (+3 years, range +2 to +5): the 7-year's nominal 2042 becomes 2045 central, so it has no headroom; the 10-year's 2045 becomes 2048. The best fps item narrowed from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20, and -2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26, so the narrowing is mostly discounting: the case has moved later, not improved (inference).

tests.name: KPI gate (doctrine; my veto) - answers the CEO's ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month or less, at least 6 months apart, after 2-3 stable months, each agreed with the FAA. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The MAX delivered 684 a year in each of 2030-34, exactly the public plan of 57 a month. No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), so my veto has nothing to act on and is not invoked. Watch item, not a live problem: CFM's public note that 80% of its shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites bears on the LEAP-1B, our sole MAX engine. Our line has not felt it. On Do Nothing the MAX runs below its 684 slots from 2037: 552 (81%), then 409-468 a year in 2038-42 (60-68%, about 34-39 a month), 521 in 2045, 618 in 2046 and 684 in 2047. The climb from about 43 to 57 a month in 2045-47 (+8, then +5.5 a month in a year) fits doctrine pacing of at most +10 a month a year. Each step will still need stable KPIs and FAA agreement in 2045-47, which the board does not model (inference).

tests.name: Two-front strain / engineering capacity (doctrine) - answers ask 2
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps window EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine window EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (both on hold): 0 years, $0, and no development in flight.

A 2035 Re-engine (window 2035-40):
- with a 2035 10-year fps (2038-45): 2 years, $1.2B, at the limit with no slack;
- with a 2035 7-year fps (2035-42): 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach.

On the board the Re-engine item falls from +2.01 alone to +1.33/+1.34 beside a 10-year fps in S1, S2 and S4, and to -2.30/-2.31 in S3. That is $0.68B for the overlap: strain plus the steeper debt penalty. On the derivative slip prior (+2 years, EIS 2042), the real overlap with a 10-year fps is 4 years ($2.4B at the board's rate), past H4.

Sequencing:
- A 2035 Re-engine clears any 2045 fps (7-year 2045-52, 10-year 2048-55) by 0 years.
- A Re-engine held to 2045 (2045-50) meets a 2045 fps at 2 years (10-year, the limit) or 5 years (7-year, a breach).
- A 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) meets a 2045 7-year by 2 years and a 10-year by 5.

So 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers:
No fps this round.

A 2035 launch:
- 7-year: EIS 2042, central 2045 on the clean-sheet prior (+3, range +2 to +5);
- 10-year: EIS 2045, central 2048.

Strain is $0 for each alone. With a 2035 Re-engine it is $3.0B for the 7-year (breach) against $1.2B for the 10-year (limit).

The 10-year beats the 7-year in every column: by $2.48-2.75B on the hold rows and by $3.03-3.32B with the Re-engine. It also has the higher worst column (-3.67 against -6.15 at Renton).

Stress-case net debt:
- every 10-year row holds at $0;
- the 7-year fails at new sites ($0.6-0.8B) and with the Re-engine (peaks $1.9-3.5B, 7 of 8 cells fail);
- the 7-year at Renton alone holds at $0.0B.

If an fps is brought, operations backs only the 10-year: it is the ramp with headroom for a clean-sheet slip. A 2045 launch gives EIS 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year).

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference) - answers ask 4
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds IP or capacity Boeing lacks, within $1B of Solo.

tests.name: Engine and supplier readiness (doctrine; supplier readiness is a hard gate) - answers ask 3
tests.threshold: Each named engine maker ready by EIS, with durability proven before EIS. Supplier output meets the rate before each rate break. A sole source is a risk to reduce.
tests.numbers:
The engine code is null with the hold.

At a launch, code 7:
- GTF2 ready 2036 and UltraFan NB ready 2037 (public record), and CFM always available;
- that is 5-9 years of margin before a 2042 or 2045 EIS, and 15-19 years before a 2052 or 2055 EIS from a 2045 launch;
- the brief's code table gives 3 fitted sources at a 2045 EIS.

Code 7 cuts our single-source exposure. Today 100% of MAX engines are CFM: LEAP-1B, about 1,368 engines a year at 684 aircraft. CFM also serves the A320neo (kept longer on Airbus's Alt plan) and NGSA. Durability proven before EIS should be a contract condition [BX-1298].

Re-engine:
- The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- RR says no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. At 6 years from launch it would be ready in 2041 at the earliest, after a 2040 EIS, so the 2040 date rests on the GEnx.
- New-part supplier gate, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]: the brief has no supplier data, so the gate is a condition at the rate break, not a fail.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2035 launch, EIS 2040 (doctrine) - answers ask 6
tests.threshold: Engineering free, Charleston capacity, engine maker and durability, supplier gate, and the type certificate before building at rate (no production-certification concurrency).
tests.numbers:
My 2030 results are re-confirmed:
- Engineering: nothing is in development, so a 2035 launch is the one development.
- Charleston: the footprint covers 787 rates in the teens. The 787 builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone Re-engine, gaining 1 pp a year from 58.8%, reaches about 108 a year (9.0 a month) in 2045, 134 (11.2) in 2060 and 145 (12.0) at the 85% cap, all inside the teens.
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- Supplier gate on new parts: a condition at the rate break.
- Certification: the type certificate comes before building at rate.
- Central EIS on the derivative prior: 2042.

H3's second half has not closed it: no A350 Re-engine is on the record. Operations does not hold the Re-engine back. Its open question is the market column S3 (-1.63), and that is not an operations test.

tests.name: Renton or new site, with the MAX bridge plan (inference) - answers ask 5
tests.threshold: Renton only alongside a launch, with a MAX bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp; otherwise new_site.
tests.numbers:
With the fps on hold, Renton changes nothing (item value 0.00), so keep new_site. There is no reason to set it before a launch: the site can change in any round before EIS, and the full ~$3.0B capex saving needs only a choice at least 3 years before EIS. Alongside a launch Renton is worth +0.36 to +0.39 (10-year) or +0.42 to +0.58 (7-year).

The risk it carries: Renton's three lines are 47 of the 57 a month. If the fps slips (clean-sheet prior +3 years) after Renton is converted, the MAX falls to the Everett North Line, at up to 15 a month (180 a year). That is a gap of up to 504 aircraft a year against 684.

Bridge plan, when Renton is chosen:
1. No Renton line converts before the fps type certificate (no concurrency).
2. Each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps line has held its rate for 2-3 stable months on KPIs.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month, about 4 years after EIS.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers are sized to the actual wind-down, not the planned one.
5. The Everett North Line carries the MAX tail, at up to 15 a month.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (inference, one remark [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column; otherwise not applicable.
tests.numbers:
There are no Rate Increase rows on this grid (it was a 2030-only order). Demand for more MAX capacity is not visible:
- the waiting backlog falls from 763 (2035) to 419 (2036) and 138 (2037), and is 0 from 2038;
- deliveries run 132-275 a year below the 684 slots in 2037-46.

Read the other way, the test says: add no MAX capacity, and keep 57 a month as the ceiling. Charleston already covers a Re-engine's widebody demand (above).

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands, and what it does to cash and net debt, as numbers rather than adjectives.
tests.numbers:
Base free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in stress).

- Do Nothing: no bill. Profit runs $0.13-0.78B a year below the game baseline in 2037-45. Net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, about $1.0B a year (7% of base free cash flow, 11% of stress), booked in 2040, with a $0.6B undiscounted debt penalty. It returns about $400M of PV per $1B of bill in S1, S2 and S4, and costs about $330M per $1B in S3. Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2035-45. Year 1 is about $3.0B (22% of base free cash flow); the peak is about $8.4B in year 7 (61% of base, 92% of stress). It costs $20M (Renton) to $26M (new site) of PV per $1B. Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- 10-year fps with the Re-engine: the two bills land together in 2035-40, plus $1.2B of strain over the 2 overlap years. That is roughly $8-9.5B a year at the 2038-40 peak, about 60-70% of base free cash flow (inference from the standard curve). Net debt is still $0.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2035-42, about $9.3B a year (67% of base, 101% of stress). It costs $57M of PV per $1B at Renton. Stress fails at new sites ($0.6-0.8B).
- Via Embraer: a peak of about $14.0B (102% of base, 152% of stress). It costs $122M of PV per $1B. Stress fails in 14 of 16 cells.

Renton avoids ~$3.0B of capex, and only with a launch.

tests.name: 2045 readiness: workforce, production system, supplier base, Renton bridge (doctrine and inference) - answers ask 7
tests.threshold: What has to happen over 2035-45 so that a 2045 launch is ready on day one, the way the strike and the 2019 delay were used to prepare?
tests.numbers:
There is no order this round; this is the plan.

1. Workforce: on Do Nothing the MAX dip (409-468 a year in 2038-42 against 684 slots) idles about a third of MAX capacity. Keep the trained workforce and redeploy it to fps production-system work and the 787, rather than shed it and rehire for 2045. The board does not price this (inference).
2. Production system: design the fps line with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before building at rate.
3. Supplier base: fund fragile suppliers through the dip. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation at 57 a month for the 2045-47 climb back. Hold engine proposals from all three makers, with durability proven before EIS, and plan on code 7.
4. Renton bridge: written by 2045 and decided with the launch, as above.
5. Sequencing: the 2045-47 MAX climb from about 43 to 57 a month and any 2045 fps launch land together. Plan one KPI-gated ask at a time.
6. If the Re-engine is still held in 2045, it meets that fps under H4 (2 years with a 10-year fps, 5 with a 7-year).

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (KPI veto NOT invoked)
vetoes.ground: No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem: the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. The KPI doctrine therefore has neither a ground nor an object this round. It would bind against any future rate step ordered while such a problem is live. The 2045-47 climb back to 57 a month should be gated step by step on KPIs and the supply of LEAP-1B engines.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto: 5 years of overlap (fps 2035-42, Re-engine 2035-40) and $3.0B of strain undiscounted, past the 2-year limit. The CEO must strike it. The same breach applies in 2045 to a 7-year fps launched in the same round as a held Re-engine.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: H4 advice, not a breach on the board: 2 years of overlap (2038-40) and $1.2B of strain, at the limit with no slack. On the +2-year derivative slip prior the real overlap is 4 years. Next to the fps, the Re-engine item falls from +2.01 to +1.33 (S1). The row sits $1.88-2.13B below the Re-engine alone in every column and $3.51B below Do Nothing in S3.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: IP advice, not binding: on the board the partner brings no IP, capacity or strain relief. It has the same EIS as the Solo 10-year, sits $10.95-11.47B below it in every column and carries a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Stress-case net debt fails in 14 of 16 cells.

vetoes.plan: fps_site: renton without a launch, or with a launch but no MAX bridge plan
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. Without a launch Renton changes nothing (0.00). With a launch it needs the bridge plan in my memo: an fps slip after conversion leaves the MAX on the Everett North Line at up to 180 a year, a gap of up to 504 aircraft a year against 684.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
KPI gate: if a quality escape, FAA scrutiny or supply-chain shortfall were reported before the orders are sealed, the gate would fail. That includes CFM's concentrated LEAP shortages reaching our line, or a LEAP-1B allocation short of 57 a month. My veto would then bind on any rate step, and I would also fail the Re-engine's supplier gate.

787 Re-engine: I would recommend launch, with operations ready for a 2035 launch and a 2040 EIS, if Malave's updated read puts the chance of an A350 Re-engine well below 28% on the bulletin's evidence and the Board accepts that S3 is not plausible this round. Two things support that: 2035 is the only zero-strain slot against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay costs about 9.5% of its value. I would move further against it on evidence of a shortfall on its new parts, a GEnx-upgrade durability gap at EIS, or a certification plan that needs production-certification concurrency.

fps: I would back a launch only on a grid where the Solo 10-year clears the Board's lines. Even then I would back only the 10-year ramp (it has headroom for the +3-year clean-sheet prior), with code 7, durability before EIS and a Renton bridge plan.

Via Embraer: only if a partner brought IP or capacity Boeing lacks at a cost within $1B of Solo. On this grid it is $10.95B or more short.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the KPI, supplier and strain gates run on operations doctrine, marked as such.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery (record, applied by inference). The MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so the KPI gate is clean (doctrine). No Rate Increase is on the menu; my veto has nothing to act on. The real job is the dip: on Do Nothing, MAX deliveries fall to 409-468 a year in 2038-42, 60-68% of our slots, and climb back to 684 by 2047. We hold the trained workforce and fund fragile suppliers through it.

Second, engineering capacity (doctrine). Holding both: zero strain. A 2035 Re-engine clears any 2045 fps by zero years. Held to 2045, it meets that fps at H4's 2-year limit, or breaks it with a 7-year ramp. Beside a 10-year fps today it sits at the limit and its value falls from +2.01 to +1.33.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth (record). Every $1B of Re-engine bill returns about $400 million in three columns and costs about $330 million in S3. Each year of later entry takes 9.5% off its value: +3.30 became +2.01 on five years of discounting alone. Embraer brings no IP or capacity we lack, at $10.95-11.47B more than Solo.

Orders: fps hold, new_site, no code; Re-engine hold. Its S3 risk is the Board's to carry. Operations does not hold it back.

other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2045 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail: Solo by default, since Pope's IP test finds Embraer adds no IP or capacity. The base case is the 10-year ramp: on this grid it beats the 7-year by $2.48-2.75B in every column and has the higher worst column. Renton comes only with Pope's MAX bridge plan, with code 7 and with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system together with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before building at rate (no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]). The case must show the item value in every column against the Board's two lines (no worse than -$1B anywhere, and above +$1B in the expected column) and Malave's slip leg as the baseline. It also sets out the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule: a 2035 launch settles at a long-run 42% (10-year) or 45% (7-year); a 2045 launch settles at 35% (7-year, EIS 2052) or 32% (10-year, EIS 2055). Sequence it under H4 against any 787 Re-engine. No date. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated)
other_moves.detail: We continue to invite all three narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Selection will be on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. With P&W's GTF2 and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB now in development, our plan is to offer customers a choice of engine at launch (code 7: CFM plus GTF2 plus UltraFan NB). No fps date and no launch commitment.

other_moves.move: Keep 787 Re-engine readiness warm (study only, no launch)
other_moves.detail: Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. The study covers engine durability, a supplier gate on new parts (rate breaks only when supplier output is there, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]) and a certification plan with the type certificate before building at rate. No programme spend is committed. Re-test it in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), and sequence it against a 2045 fps under H4: a same-round 10-year fps sits at the 2-year limit, and a 7-year fps breaches it.

other_moves.move: Hold the 737 at 57 a month with KPI gates and stability first
other_moves.detail: No rate step. KPIs are monitored monthly. 57 a month is the ceiling. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, treat CFM's concentrated sub-tier shortages as a watch item, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place. Any future step is gated one at a time on KPIs and FAA agreement.

other_moves.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers through any demand dip
other_moves.detail: If MAX deliveries run below the 57-a-month slots, keep trained people and redeploy them to fps production-system work and the 787 rather than shed and rehire. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible [BX-1243, B-2330], so supplier readiness is never why a 2045 programme slips. This is the way we used the strike and the 2019 delay to prepare [BX-1258, BX-1225].

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board, with headroom kept for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year). Nothing is said publicly.

decision.public_statement:
Back in 2025 I said we were turning the ship but hadn't turned it. I think we've turned it now. The balance sheet is repaired and staying repaired. The 737 line has built at 57 a month to plan for five straight years. The 777X and the MAX family are delivering. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here, and the job now is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. We'll do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. We've looked hard at it with the data in front of us, and the case isn't there yet. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we do go, we build it at rate the right way. With new engines in development at Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and CFM always at the table, we expect to give our customers a choice of engine, with durability proven before entry into service. When we launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year either. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

On production, the 737 stays at 57 a month and stays stable. Any step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We're keeping our trained people and our suppliers ready. Going slow has let us go faster, and stability is what lets us move when the time comes.

Our dates will be set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see. This is the frame's lean, confirmed by both memos.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. Pope's KPI gate is clean and her veto is not invoked. No Rate Increase is on the menu. CFM's sub-tier shortages are a watch item, not a live problem.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1303]
   - Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress on every 10-year row.
   - Technology: ready by EIS. GTF2 is ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037, CFM always.
   - Market: not ready on this grid. No fps row beats Do Nothing in any column.
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's slip leg, S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01, line -3.01):
   - Pass: Do Nothing, the Re-engine and the four 10-year rows.
   - Fail (binding): every 7-year and via-Embraer row.
   This round S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so the leg works as a level test.
   Pope's priors are unpriced but point the same way: a clean-sheet +3 years puts a 10-year fps at 2048; a derivative +2 years puts the Re-engine at 2042.
4. Is this doing less, better? [BX-1239] Yes. Do Nothing beats every fps row by $1.20B or more in every column. The only plans within ε of it in S1 (10-year + Re-engine rows) have worst columns $3.51-3.88B lower.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding buffer veto strikes every 7-year and via-Embraer row. None was ordered.
- Pope's H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is honoured: not ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto: no object this round.
- I decided the rest. No overrides.

fps: HOLD
- The best row, 10-year at Renton, gives up $1.20 / $1.46 / $1.20 / $1.22B (S1 to S4).
- My debt-first test needs a plan more than ε ahead of Do Nothing in S1. It is $2.20B short. The Board's -$1B per-item line fails in every column.
- An objective premium of $1.20B (S1) would sit inside my $2B cap. I won't use it: it would carry an item that fails my own test and the Board's line. 50/50 is the company's mission, not on my ranked list.
- Pope's discounting check shows the narrowing from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20 is mostly five years of discounting (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26). The case has moved later; it has not got better.
- Cost of waiting, said plainly. There is no 2040 round, so the earliest fps EIS becomes 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year). Under the lead-edge rule the long-run share falls from 42-45% (a 2035 launch) to 32-35% (a 2045 launch).
- The grid assumes nobody moves later, so it cannot price a 2045 launch. Malave confirms nothing in the brief puts a dollar figure on it. It is information for the 2045 case, not a reason to launch now. Airbus's 2037 date does not set ours [B-2313, B-2315].
- Ramp and route for 2045: the 10-year ramp, Solo. The 7-year fails the buffer and stress debt at new sites. Via Embraer sits $10.95-11.47B behind Solo with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty, and Pope finds it adds no IP or capacity.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call)
- Item value: +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4; -1.63 in S3. It passes Malave's buffer by $2.01B and debt holds at $0. In my expected column it is the best plan.
- Three grounds move me to hold:
  (a) The Board will veto it under its -$1B per-item line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine: Airbus says 'A350 family', and RR is waiting with a widebody UltraFan for 'a Re-engine on the table'. I have no override against the Board. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
  (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], has updated his read on the evidence: from 40-50% to about 30% (25-35%). That puts the weighted edge at +$0.92B ($0.74-1.10B). At the centre that is inside ε, so the higher worst column decides: Do Nothing -2.47 against -4.10. He also notes the +2.01 is a ceiling: it assumes Airbus never re-engines later.
  (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low. A launch now is a one-way door, since the EIS is 2040 and there is no round before it (H5).
- I'm not hiding what the hold costs. Pope shows 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay takes about 9.5% off its value. A 2045 Re-engine would meet a 2045 fps at H4's limit, so this hold may in practice close the programme.
- The cost is logged separately, as a Board-downside hold and not against the cap: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4; $1.63B saved in S3; $0.92B weighted at 30%.
- My reading of Airbus's probability is Low confidence on my record. I relied on Malave's read and on company doctrine (profile §7, the A330neo precedent [B-2446]).

SITE, CODE, RATE
- fps_site: new_site. Renton is worth 0.00 without a launch, and the full $3.0B capex saving needs only a choice 3 years before EIS.
- Engine code: null with the hold. At launch it will be code 7: three sources, all ready by EIS, an allowed pair against NGSA. That is doctrine and my public requirement; I have no record as Boeing CEO on engine choice.
- rate_737: hold, the only value. The ceiling stays at 57.

HARD RULES AND RED LINES
- H1: the 2030 ruling stands and is not re-made.
- H3, first half: lifted in 2030. Second half: in force. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the 787 Re-engine stays open but is held.
- H4: respected, with no development in flight.
- H5: nothing to cancel.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: soft total $0.
- H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- My own red lines are all respected: no concurrency, no fixed-price development, no FAA blame, no attribution of supplier problems to Airbus.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): -1.01 / -0.02 / -2.47 / -1.01.
- No Board items: fps, re787 and fps_site are each at their default, so every item value is 0.00.
- Expected column: S1. Risk case S4 is -1.01: 0.00 against Do Nothing, with $2.00B of headroom over -3.01. Buffer: pass.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547], and net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060. The grid holds the fps back, not the cash.
- Pope's gates: KPI clean; zero strain; engines ready by any EIS; no concurrency; Renton not chosen, with a bridge plan drafted for 2045.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine is logged as a Board-downside hold.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- the A350 probability (via Malave);
- engine code 7;
- the Renton bridge plan;
- the slip priors.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input on the Re-engine, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer: accepted to the cent. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows are struck. The 10-year rows pass, but at new sites with only $0.39B of headroom.
- Net debt: accepted from the metrics table. The debt penalty is already netted and not subtracted again.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass, accepted.
- Cash timing: accepted. The 10-year peaks at $8.44B in 2041, 92% of stress free cash flow. In cash, a same-round Re-engine falls entirely inside the fps spend.
- What moved me: his updated A350 read of about 30%, which he moved down on two of his own 2030 triggers. It puts the weighted edge just inside ε, so the higher worst column decides. That supports the Board's line rather than standing in for it.
- I log his offer: he would support the Re-engine on evidence that puts the A350 chance below 28%. That is the trigger to carry forward.
- His point that +2.01 is an undiscounted ceiling (it assumes no later A350 move) is noted.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I took her memo as gates and facts, not judgement.
- Accepted: the KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object; the 737 ceiling stays at 57. Strain is zero on the hold; a 2035 10-year + Re-engine pair sits at H4's limit, and a 7-year pair breaches it. Engines for code 7 are ready 5-9 years before EIS. Via Embraer fails the partner test. Re-engine readiness passes on the GEnx upgrade.
- Two of her findings sharpened the rationale. Her discounting check (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26) shows the fps case has moved later, not improved. And 2035 is the only zero-strain Re-engine slot against a 2045 fps, so I've said plainly that the hold may close it.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan and her 2045 readiness plan (workforce through the dip, fragile suppliers, production system proven at rate, one KPI-gated ask at a time) go into the other moves.
- Her statement that operations does not hold the Re-engine back is accepted. The hold rests on the market column S3 and the Board's line, not on readiness.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1: rivals hold. Airbus keeps its Alt plan; per the bulletin it reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event, and none is on the record. No A350 Re-engine.
- S2 (Airbus back on its base plan) is the upside.
- S3 (an A350 Re-engine, about 30% on Malave's read) is the plausible downside.
- S4 (Delay Tactics) is the risk case. It equals S1 on every hold row.
The column values our plan; it does not set our dates [B-2313].
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (+1.00). I chose fps: hold + 787: hold (-1.01), $2.01B below it. That is a Board-downside hold: the Board's -$1B per-item line binds while S3 (-1.63) is not ruled out, and I have no override. It is logged separately and not against the cap. Weighted at Malave's 30% read of an A350 Re-engine, the gap is $0.92B, inside ε, where the higher worst column (-2.47 against -4.10) decides.
decision.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0. Objective premium: $0.
- fps hold: no premium, because the grid prefers it. The best fps row (10-year at Renton) sits $1.20B below Do Nothing in S1 and $1.46B below in S2. Launching it for 50/50, incumbency or the engine enabler would be an objective premium of $1.20B. That is inside the cap, but it fails my debt-first test and the Board's -$1B line, so it is not taken.
- 787 Re-engine hold: a known cost, logged separately as a Board-downside hold, as the Board asked. It gives up $2.01B in S1, S2 and S4 and saves $1.63B in S3. Weighted at Malave's 30% (25-35%), the cost is $0.92B ($0.74-1.10B).
- What breaks the number: if the A350 does not re-engine, the hold gives up the full $2.01B. If it does, the hold saves $1.63B, and H3 closes the 787 Re-engine for good.
decision.objective_note:
The objectives never change the payoff.
- Hold the 50/50 split: unmet on every hold plan. Preference share falls to 37% at NGSA's 2037 EIS and 20% from 2043. Not chased: the premium needed would breach the Board's line and my own debt-first test.
- Defend incumbency: unmet (worst year 20%). Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45 and recovers to 36.3% from 2047, when Airbus's capacity binds. This is the long-cycle stake the 2045 fps case must answer. Waiting costs share: 42-45% for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch. The grid does not price it.
- Balance sheet, repair and keep repaired (base and stress): met. Net debt is $0 from 2029 through 2050.
- Engine enabler, three makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, RR).
- Engine enabler, two or three sources on our narrowbody: unmet, since the MAX flies CFM only. It is answered at launch by code 7 and by the public, dateless engine-sourcing requirement.
decision.predictions:
AIRBUS
- NGSA enters service in 2037 on schedule, and Airbus keeps the Alt plan (S1).
- An A350 Re-engine this round is about 30% (Malave's read). Airbus's engineering is on NGSA first, but its 'A350 family' wording and RR's waiting widebody UltraFan keep it open.
- No Delay Tactics effect: with no fps they would be 'naked' and draw a $48.32B fine, and S4 equals S1 on our hold.

ENGINE MAKERS
- GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both fitted to NGSA.
- CFM keeps the LEAP-1B on the MAX.
- No widebody UltraFan, since no Re-engine is on the table.

OUR RESULTS IF NOBODY MOVES AGAIN
- ΔPV: -1.01 (S1), -0.02 (S2), -2.47 (S3), -1.01 (S4).
- Net debt $0 in base and stress at every check year.
- NB preference share 37% in 2037 and 20% from 2043.
- MAX deliveries 409-468 a year in 2038-42, back to 684 from 2047.
- WB share 58.8%.

2045
- Bring the staged fps case: Solo, the 10-year ramp, Renton with a bridge plan, code 7, against the Board's two lines and Malave's slip leg.
- Re-test the 787 Re-engine only if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced under H4.

board_response.response: Taken. Objective premium $0, soft premium $0. Launching the 10-year at Renton would have needed $1.20B (S1) to $1.46B (S2). First and foremost, the KPI gate (doctrine [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308]). The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. CFM's note that 80% of its shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites is still a watch item, not a live problem.
