public_statements.boeing:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. We have, and the job now is to keep it steady. The balance sheet is repaired and it's staying repaired. The 777X and the 737 MAX family are delivering, and the 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class.

On the 737, we're bringing the line back to full output, 57 a month, as demand comes back. We'll take that one step at a time. Each step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity, and when we and the FAA agree the line is ready. We'll make sure our suppliers and our engine supply are there before each step. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

On a new airplane: we're not launching one this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. I'll tell you plainly what's changed. The market case is better than it was. It isn't there yet. We will do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready. The market is getting there, but it hasn't got there. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we go, we go on a conservative plan with headroom in it, with no fixed-price development risk, and we build it at rate the right way.

On engines, we've updated our requirement. Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are now one Joint Venture, so our plan is to give customers a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. We'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

Our dates are set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, and its production ramp-up is now reaching its planned rate. We will continue a disciplined and controlled ramp-up: every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family is completing an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The new aircraft was funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041, and it's on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We hold that engine to the standard our customers set and we set for ourselves: durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included. Test and field data go to our customers and our Board first. They don't go into a press line.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

Boeing has invited us to bring a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support, the GTF and the new engine together.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block. It would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated to the record)
boeing.detail: We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. With GTF2 and UltraFan NB now folded into the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

boeing.move: 737 MAX back to full output at 57 a month, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
boeing.detail: As demand comes back, the 737 returns to its 57-a-month ceiling. This is not a Rate Increase. Each step is taken one at a time, only after stable KPIs and agreement with the FAA, and only when supplier and engine output for the next step is proven. No step dates are published.

boeing.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
boeing.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for NGSA at rate
airbus.detail:
This continues the round-1 and round-2 programme, now for NGSA in steady production.
- The NGSA wing stays in-house.
- Aerostructures come through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites.
- Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts.
- The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist continues.
It serves our own production only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: NGSA engine supply: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, at our own volumes
airbus.detail:
NGSA is fitted with CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine. That is two sources from three engine makers.
- The capacity agreements with both cover only our own NGSA volumes (and the A320neo tail), with no exclusivity and nothing above our own production.
- The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Prepare the next step in industrial capacity, gated on safety, quality and supply
airbus.detail:
Our own factory ceiling now limits deliveries, and the waiting backlog is growing. We prepare the step and do not commit to it.
- Capacity talks with both engine sources, for our own extra volumes only. No exclusivity, and nothing drawn from any rival's engine allocation.
- The in-house wing and the Aubert & Duval titanium and forgings are sized first.
- Staffing comes from our own skills pipeline.
The step is taken only once:
- NGSA holds its current rate on its KPIs with no open quality finding;
- both engine sources commit capacity;
- no supply crunch is reported.
In public we give no rate number and no date, only a gate. Internally, the capex comes to the Audit Committee as its own line against the $5.2B peak-cash line, and to the Board as an item if it exceeds EUR 300m (Toepfer's flag, Wagner's conditions).

airbus.move: Orderly completion of the A320neo family transition
airbus.detail: The Alt plan runs out as planned. The last A320neo family aircraft are built to customer demand, and NGSA has first claim on resources. No rate number is published.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue working with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

airbus.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2040s
airbus.detail: We continue apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe. They staff NGSA production at rate, the capacity step being prepared and future widebody work from our own pipeline. The programmes do no targeted hiring from any rival's team [AX-0073, A-0330].

cfm.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
cfm.detail: H5: no cancel and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. Continuing it as technology with Safran is joint practice. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP [CX-0162]. The one RISE allowance stays unused.

cfm.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of everything else
cfm.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it [CX-0613, CX-0540].

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet first: the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and the GTF fleet; Hot Section kit sold at value; fleet spares ahead of new hardware
pratt_whitney.detail:
The fleet comes before any new hardware [PX-0080][PX-0084].
- The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100].
- Fleet spares and MRO material are allocated ahead of NGSA OE and ahead of any Joint Venture block hardware when they compete for the same parts.
- We fix forward through shop-visit upgrades. Any durability fix for the NGSA engine enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.
- Pacing parts and spares for the gear and the core are being sized to every Joint Venture engine that carries them, not only to our counted share, and to the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits.
- OE allocation is agreed jointly with Airbus, and we tell Airbus early where we fall short [PX-0099][PX-0066].
No date is given for any ramp or recovery. The move has no effect on the game board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture governed to its published terms; 'never' restated as the public floor
pratt_whitney.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms we published in 2035, restated with one change: the Finance routing comes out of the public text.
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233].
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

pratt_whitney.move: Standing offer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts
pratt_whitney.detail:
This answers Boeing's standing invitation to all three engine makers. We offer the Joint Venture engine, which has been ready since 2036, in the standard now in service. It is offered on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100], and the same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer.
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing either way.

rolls_royce.move: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing and durability work continues inside a flat R&D envelope
rolls_royce.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and life-limited part extensions on the installed fleet. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat envelope, not added. This is our answer on the widebody, not a new programme. No widebody programme is launched [RX-0123, RX-0214, RX-0101].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops: live for the NGSA fleet and sized for a second airframe
rolls_royce.detail: Partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team. The plan is Rolls-Royce's own. It is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe before that airframe enters service. Our partner's shops add capacity after that and never replace this plan. No dates are disclosed [RX-0283, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: Answer to Boeing's engine-sourcing invitation, renewed
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce offers its part of the Joint Venture engine for a future Boeing single-aisle, on standard terms, with no launch discount and no concession. Durability proven before entry into service, as a contract condition. Support and MRO through partner shops in place before entry into service. No dates and no new spend. Rolls-Royce speaks only for its own part [RX-0058, RX-0081, RX-0283].

rolls_royce.move: Standard commercial terms only
rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

rolls_royce.move: Capital allocation frame
rolls_royce.detail: Cash from the Trent and Joint Venture fleets goes first to the balance sheet, then to a 30-40% dividend payout, then to investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0242, RX-0213, RX-0215, RX-0261].

boeing.move: Staged fps business case for the 2050 round (authority-to-offer work)
boeing.detail:
Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP or capacity we lack: its partnership is with CFM, and via Embraer sits $4.04-4.23B below the Solo 10-year.

The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.88-1.14 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.

Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation follows the actual wind-down.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.

Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. Type certificate before rate; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

The case must show:
- the item value in S1, S2 and S3 against the Board's two lines;
- Malave's slip leg as the baseline, with the clean-sheet prior (+3 years) and a cost-overrun sensitivity (does the item survive a 2% overrun?) priced in full, once;
- the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule.

Decide the fps and the 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4: both held to 2050 gives 2 years with a 10-year fps and 5 with a 7-year. If the 2050 case does not clear, we say so and do not force it.

boeing.move: MAX climb-back ladder and supplier gates (internal plan)
Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded through the climb
boeing.detail: Bring back the trained people kept through the 2038-44 dip, and train for the ladder first. Then form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers that carry 52 and 57 are the ones a 2050 fps would load next.

boeing.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
boeing.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: the item has shrunk by ten years of discounting (2.01 in 2035 to 0.74 now), and a 2050 launch is about +0.45, below ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine. This hold very probably closes it on this board.

Re-test it in 2050 only if H3's second half is still open (no A350 Re-engine on the record), and only as one pair with any fps under H4. No programme spend is committed.

boeing.move: No shareholder-return signal
boeing.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board. Keep headroom for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.44B in its peak year, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

airbus.move: NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
airbus.detail: The review continues through the ramp and into steady state. It now carries a standing watch item on the Joint Venture engine: durability and full life on life-limited parts, with GTF2's tested configuration first and Rolls-Royce content on a later block after its own durability proof. CFM remains the backstop source. Any quality finding goes to the Board at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AG-0038].

airbus.move: Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review
Audit Committee: net cash, rating and returns
airbus.detail:
Toepfer reports on a proxy that he labels as such. Net cash has rebuilt from a trough of about +$0.3B at end-2037 to above FY2025's $13.4B by 2042, and to about $32-46B by end-2045.
- The A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout are fundable with no raise and no cut.
- Any new buyback or change to shareholder returns comes to the Board as a reserved matter, with the figures shown.
[AX-0104, AX-0102, A-0402, AG-0062]

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine: held at the 2045 gate, with the stopping test recorded
airbus.detail:
It is not tabled. Two tests stopped it:
- Toepfer's binding robustness test: the item is -0.50 in S6/S7 and short of $1B in every column.
- The company's own launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), which is met in no column.
It stays an internal study. It comes back only if the record offers one of these:
- a grid gain of at least $1B over hold;
- S6/S7 ruled out on the public record;
- a widebody engine committed in time.
It always carries the rule-3 check. A Boeing 787 Re-engine on the record would close it. No public widebody-engine invitation is issued while it is not tabled, and no timing is disclosed [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253].

cfm.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's updated sourcing invitation for its next single-aisle, through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: We offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted, ready since 2041), with a LEAP derivative as the floor (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. We accept durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition; it's our own standard. We stand behind what test and field data back: the LEAP-1A kit, certified in December 2024, in every LEAP-1A delivery, more than doubling time on wing [CX-0209, CX-0225]. The Ducted's hot-and-harsh and dust results go to Boeing only as the cross-functional team releases them, and we make no Ducted durability claim before then (Ali, H6). No price, no concession, no number. Any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty goes to Safran first and is modelled conservatively [CX-0184, CX-0979]. No ready year earlier than 2041, and no year by which durability will be 'proven'.

cfm.move: Confirm Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation at today's rate (57 a month) as a ceiling for supply certainty, through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: Confirmed only once Safran agrees, with no price in it [CX-0184, CX-0160]. It's a backlog we share [CX-0197], and we won't get ahead of Boeing or the FAA on any rate step [CX-0307]. We plan to deliveries, not to the ceiling: the 737 took 818-936 LEAP-1B engines a year since 2038, 60-68% of the 1,368 a year that 57 a month would take. That's lean before capital, and it means no overcapitalisation (Ghai) [CX-0540].

cfm.move: Airbus long-term capacity agreements (A320neo and NGSA, from 2035): confirm status and close any open item through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: Product and supply only, on standard terms. Any price term is a joint decision, with no number before Safran agrees [CX-0184]. Scope as Airbus states it publicly: its own A320neo and NGSA volumes, no exclusivity, nothing above its own ramp, with NGSA's first claim respected. Whether the agreements are signed is not on our record. Ghai reports the signature status to the Board.

cfm.move: Partner Embraer: terms worked through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: No Embraer number goes to the market or to an airframer until terms are agreed with Safran (Ghai's condition) [CX-0184].

cfm.move: Close the three durability evidence gaps cross-functionally and report them to the Board
Supplier-floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages, reported to the Board before any new load
cfm.detail: This is the third time the Board has asked, and it's still not met. I own it with Ali. We show the floor margin for LEAP, the kits and the Ducted together, and any new programme load is gated on that data. Kits and the LEAP rate come first. We build LEAP-1B to deliveries, not to the ceiling. This follows doctrine (lean before capital), because Ali's floor record ends in 2025 [CX-0613, CX-0540, CX-0653].

cfm.move: Report the Ducted's 2035-2040 cash spend to the Board from the ledger
cfm.detail: The board books $6.0B ($4.0B of R&D in 2035 plus $2.0B of strain) against $6.0B approved, with no overrun and no write-off. The yearly cash curve isn't in our brief, so Ghai reports it from the ledger against the $1.0B a year approved and the 2-3% band.

pratt_whitney.move: In-service durability report and the Rolls-Royce block gate to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Eddy brings the data as they exist, and says so plainly where they do not yet exist:
(a) time on wing against plan, split by operating environment;
(b) removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage;
(c) severe-environment and fleet-leader findings;
(d) every life-limited part's life against full life, with any life-limit reduction;
(e) configuration percentages, AOG count, shop-visit rate, turn times and the pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly.
If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so, and we contain the problem before any new commitment.

The Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule:
- Configuration control: a joint configuration board, with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core.
- Spares: no intermix in shop visits until the block is certified and its own spares are stocked.
- Testing: at least Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme) at severe-environment conditions [PX-0084][PX-0128]. Time on wing must be no worse than the fitted standard, with interface load tests on our gear and core.
- Parts: full-life parts at entry into service.
- Supply and support: Rolls-Royce's parts capacity qualified before rate, and its support in place before entry into service.
The data go to the committee, and the block waits for its clearance. No date is given. If the data are late, the block waits.

pratt_whitney.move: Annual whole-programme NPV review to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
From Mitchill's memo.

(a) Booked figure: -0.14 = engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted. 'Capitalise on the GTF' is reported as not met.

(b) The bridge from +0.48 (2035) is -0.62, all of it engine value. As PV at 2026:
- 2037-41: +0.11;
- 2042-44: -0.18 (936 engines against 976 in 2044);
- 2045-56: -0.56 (876 a year against 920).
Derived reading of the public tables, labelled inference: the fold and the equal-share rule cost nothing against the S1 path (our 2041 NGSA share of 38.4% matches the projection). From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half of it from us. That is about 44 engines a year.

(c) The end-state share of 23.3% is derived as 876 engines out of 3,768 NB engines (NGSA at 100 a month plus the MAX at 57, all CFM). Against the 2035 S4 projection (+2.63) the gap is -2.77. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed: 2041 came in at exactly the S1 figure.

(d) S2 sits -0.59 below S1. A Boeing fps puts NGSA under the two-airframe share rule while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The brief has no S2 year table, so the gap cannot be placed by year.

(e) Comparisons:
- Against a buyback (PV 0): -0.14, not met.
- Against Do Nothing: no row in this brief. The direction only: from 2046 all 876 engines a year fly on NGSA.
- Derived return with R&D discounted at 10% (ratable $0.33B a year over 2030-35): about +0.77, with a range of +0.49 to +1.01. Labelled derived, for Finance only, never booked and never public.

pratt_whitney.move: Enterprise risk register update to the Audit Committee and the full Board
pratt_whitney.detail:
Retire the 2035 risk that Airbus moves NGSA to code 5. It is moot: NGSA is in service with P&W fitted.

Add three risks:
(1) In-service durability and time on wing of the NGSA engine. It now holds the credibility objective, and no fleet data are yet in the brief.
(2) Share pressure from CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership.
(3) Joint Venture alignment with Rolls-Royce: its 'own test programme' for the folded UltraFan and its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing.

Watch item: gear-and-core pacing parts sized to the whole Joint Venture flow (about 1,750 modules a year, derived) and to the GTF shop base (about 12,100 engines since 2026, derived).

pratt_whitney.move: Written alignment confirmation sought from Rolls-Royce; any cash or block cost to Finance as a capital item
pratt_whitney.detail:
We ask Rolls-Royce to confirm in writing two things. First, that UltraFan content enters only as a later block on the Joint Venture engine, through the joint team and our gate. Second, that any Boeing offer it makes is the Joint Venture engine.

A block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine. It would be the alignment break, and a Board-level risk [P-1875].

Any Rolls-Royce request for a technology credit in cash beyond equal shares, any block integration cost beyond equal shares, and any fleet-cost overrun return to Finance as a capital item. Mitchill would veto the first on ground 3. This routing stays in the private record.

pratt_whitney.move: Counsel review of the GTF paragraph before release
pratt_whitney.detail: The GTF time-on-wing paragraph in the public statement goes to counsel before release, given the derivative claims over GTF oversight. No figure is added beyond the bulletin's public facts and Mitchill's checked wording.

rolls_royce.move: Rolls-Royce-module durability gates reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round
rolls_royce.detail: Watson reports the gates with no date: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. Our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service; no pacing bent to any airframer's ramp; no concession to P&W or any airframer. P&W's GTF hot-and-sandy time-on-wing record is the watch item. If a gate fails, the block waits and we tell Airbus and P&W early [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476, R-0970].

rolls_royce.move: Widebody watch for 2050
rolls_royce.detail: If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, the ExCo brings one row, A350 first, on the 2050 grid with its item value, worst column against its own bill and the $5B strain shown. Bars (team doctrine, inference): the upgrade needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB needs a Re-engine on the record and at least +$4B weighted before the strain, so its shortfall sits inside the $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column. Otherwise the core is protected through time on wing.

other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2050 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail:
Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP or capacity we lack: its partnership is with CFM, and via Embraer sits $4.04-4.23B below the Solo 10-year.

The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.88-1.14 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.

Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation follows the actual wind-down.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.

Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. Type certificate before rate; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

The case must show:
- the item value in S1, S2 and S3 against the Board's two lines;
- Malave's slip leg as the baseline, with the clean-sheet prior (+3 years) and a cost-overrun sensitivity (does the item survive a 2% overrun?) priced in full, once;
- the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule.

Decide the fps and the 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4: both held to 2050 gives 2 years with a 10-year fps and 5 with a 7-year. If the 2050 case does not clear, we say so and do not force it.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated to the record)
other_moves.detail: We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. With GTF2 and UltraFan NB now folded into the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX back to full output at 57 a month, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
other_moves.detail: As demand comes back, the 737 returns to its 57-a-month ceiling. This is not a Rate Increase. Each step is taken one at a time, only after stable KPIs and agreement with the FAA, and only when supplier and engine output for the next step is proven. No step dates are published.

other_moves.move: MAX climb-back ladder and supplier gates (internal plan)
Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded through the climb
other_moves.detail: Bring back the trained people kept through the 2038-44 dip, and train for the ladder first. Then form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers that carry 52 and 57 are the ones a 2050 fps would load next.

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
other_moves.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: the item has shrunk by ten years of discounting (2.01 in 2035 to 0.74 now), and a 2050 launch is about +0.45, below ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine. This hold very probably closes it on this board.

Re-test it in 2050 only if H3's second half is still open (no A350 Re-engine on the record), and only as one pair with any fps under H4. No programme spend is committed.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board. Keep headroom for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.44B in its peak year, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. We have, and the job now is to keep it steady. The balance sheet is repaired and it's staying repaired. The 777X and the 737 MAX family are delivering, and the 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class.

On the 737, we're bringing the line back to full output, 57 a month, as demand comes back. We'll take that one step at a time. Each step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity, and when we and the FAA agree the line is ready. We'll make sure our suppliers and our engine supply are there before each step. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

On a new airplane: we're not launching one this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. I'll tell you plainly what's changed. The market case is better than it was. It isn't there yet. We will do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready. The market is getting there, but it hasn't got there. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we go, we go on a conservative plan with headroom in it, with no fixed-price development risk, and we build it at rate the right way.

On engines, we've updated our requirement. Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are now one Joint Venture, so our plan is to give customers a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. We'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

Our dates are set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.
- Submitted row: -1.01 / -1.34 / -1.01 (S1 / S2 / S3).
- Nothing differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer veto binds on all four via-Embraer rows (S3 -4.68 to -5.13, 1.67-2.12 past the -3.01 line). None is chosen.
- The KPI doctrine has no object: rate_737 is hold only, and no problem is live.
- Pope flagged H4 on the 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years) and on a 10-year fps now with a 2050 Re-engine (5 years). Neither is chosen.
- No flag needs a strike, and there are no overrides.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271]. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
2. Market, technology and Boeing all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
   - Technology: yes. CFM is always ready, and the Joint Venture has been ready since 2036.
   - Balance sheet: yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress, the 777X turned in 2029 [BX-0547], and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' gate passes for any 10-year row.
   - Market: turning, not turned. Demand above both makers' slots from 2047 moved the fps item from -1.20 to +0.07, about $0.51B of it real. That is still a tie, not a case [BX-1300].
3. What if certification takes longer? S3 equals S1 on every row, so the printed slip leg prices nothing. Malave priced the slip instead:
   - fps: on the clean-sheet prior of +3 years, any slip cost above about $1.0B (1.7% of the bill) turns the 10-year at Renton negative. The 777X reset alone was $4.9B [BX-0550].
   - Pope: a 2.1% overrun erases it on its own.
   - Re-engine: the derivative prior takes it to +0.61.
   So I plan for the reset, once [BX-1318, BX-1319], and the fps edge does not survive it.
4. Doing less, better [BX-1239]? Every plan within ε of Do Nothing in S1 (+0.74, +0.56, +0.41, +0.07, -0.08, ...) loses to doing less. Do Nothing is also the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]: it has nothing to slip.

DEBT FIRST (the grid already nets the penalty; not subtracted again)
- No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in S1.
- Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B against a $0.07B netted edge; Re-engine $0.6B.

TIE-BREAK ON WORST COLUMN
Malave reports plainly that on the printed grid the 10-year at Renton has the higher worst column (S2 -1.27 against -1.34). That $0.07B edge equals the item value at a nominal 2055 date and a nominal bill, and goes with any slip cost above about $1.0B. My first tie-break is doing less, and his slip-priced test also picks Do Nothing.

PER-ROW RESULTS (item values S1 / S2 / S3 against the default)
- Re-engine alone: +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74.
  - Best in S1, but inside ε and below the Board's +$1B line, whatever the probability p of an A350 Re-engine (0.74 - 1.55p).
  - Its worst column, -2.15, is 0.81 below Do Nothing's.
  - Board hold, logged separately.
- 10-year at Renton: +0.07 in every column; at new sites -0.08.
  - Fails my debt-first ε and the Board's +$1B line by $0.93B.
  - Passes buffer (S3 -0.94, headroom +2.07), Downside, H4 and net debt $0 in base and stress.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.56 / -0.99 / +0.56 against Do Nothing.
  - Its Re-engine item falls to -1.06 in S2, which fails the Board's Downside line.
  - H4 sits at its 2-year limit with no slack, and reaches 4 years on a 2-year derivative slip.
- 7-year rows: closed. They sit 0.88-1.14 below the 10-year. Stress net debt fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B). With the Re-engine they breach H4 at 5 years, and their strain window lands on the MAX climb (Pope).
- Via Embraer: closed by Malave's binding veto. It is $4.04-4.23B below Solo, carries a $52.5B undiscounted penalty, fails stress ($1.5-6.3B) and fails Pope's IP test.

RED LINES AND HARD RULES
- H1 and H3's first half: lifted in my 2030 ruling, not re-made.
- H3's second half: confirmed open. No A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4, H5, H6 and H8: respected. Soft total $0.07B.
- Mine: no production-certification concurrency, no fixed-price development, and no step in the MAX climb without stable KPIs.

COST OF WAITING (information, not a reason)
- On the grid, about $0.03B: a 2050 launch is worth at most about +0.04.
- In share under the lead-edge rule, unscored and after 2050: the long-run split falls from 32% (10-year now, EIS 2055) or 35% (7-year now, EIS 2052) to 27% (10-year, EIS 2060) or 30% (7-year, EIS 2057).
- I say it honestly: on this board's demand path the fps may never clear the Board's line, and this hold very probably closes the 787 Re-engine.
- Building a new future is on my list [BX-1245]; chasing share is not, and Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

RECORD VS DOCTRINE
- My record drove: the hold (doing less [BX-1239]; three streams [BX-1296]; slip planning [BX-1319]); the KPI-gated, FAA-agreed climb [BX-1259, BX-1322]; and keeping suppliers funded [BX-1243].
- Doctrine drove: code 7 in the engine requirement (Low confidence: I have no record on engine choice); the 10-year/Renton base for 2050; logging the Re-engine as a Board hold; and the A350 probability read, which is Malave's and doctrine.

BIASES: stability over share, under-disclosure (no dates, ladder kept internal), and cash for readiness are all displayed at no grid cost.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Jay's memo was weighed heavily on estimates, the buffer and the slip, as my independent check [BX-1316]. It is a thin seat, though: his record is one call (Low), so beyond the buffer test his views are inference or doctrine, and I treated them as advice.

Taken as binding:
- The buffer veto on every via-Embraer row (S3 -4.68 to -5.13). Accepted; none is chosen.

Taken as decisive input:
- The slip pricing. On the +3-year clean-sheet prior, a slip cost above about $1.0B turns the 10-year at Renton negative, which removes its $0.07B edge in S2.
- The 'Fundable when the 777X turns' pass, and the net-debt line ($0 in base and stress on every 10-year row, the Re-engine and Do Nothing).
- The cost of waiting: about $0.03B on the grid, a 2050 fps at most about +0.04, and a 2050 Re-engine about +0.45.

Taken as advice:
- His A350 read moving from 30% to about 25% (doctrine, not his record). It changes no order, since the Re-engine never clears ε at any p.
- His balance-sheet tie-break.

His printed-grid Meet-and-beat result goes against Do Nothing by $0.07B, and I report it to the Board as he did. I resolve it on doing less first and on his own slip-priced test second.
memo_weighing.ops:
Stephanie's seat runs on operations doctrine (Very low airplane-business evidence; her record is Global Services), so I took her results as facts against the brief, not as judgement on the airplane case.

Accepted:
- The KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object.
- The four-step ladder for the MAX climb (42 / 47 / 52 / 57), gated on KPIs, FAA agreement, firm orders, and supplier output proven before 52 and 57. Adopted as an internal plan.
- Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation for 1,368 a year before the 47 step.
- Her H4 table, including the case my frame missed: a 7-year fps now with a 2050 Re-engine gives 2 years. With the slip priors, no pair has slack.
- The 2.1% overrun sensitivity, which strengthens the hold.
- Her IP test: Embraer adds no airframe IP or capacity, so via Embraer fails.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan, carried into the 2050 case. Renton is worth 0.00 on a hold, so the site stays new_site.
- Her 2050 readiness list.

She is clear that operations does not hold the Re-engine back; the business case does. I record it that way.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold).
- No A350 Re-engine has come since 2030, and Airbus repeats that its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. Malave's doctrine read puts an A350 Re-engine at about 25% (range 20-30%).
- S2 (Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine) is the plausible downside and the worst column on every row.

boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (-0.27 in S1; -2.15 in S2; -0.27 in S3).

Not taken:
- Its edge over Do Nothing is +0.74 in S1, inside ε ($1B) and below the Board's +$1B business-case line, which would veto it.
- Weighted at Malave's 25%, the edge is +0.35.
- Its worst column (-2.15) is 0.81 below Do Nothing's.
- Doing less wins inside ε [BX-1239].

The hold gives up $0.74B in S1 and S3 and saves $0.81B in S2. It is logged separately as a Board hold.
boeing.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0.07B. Objective premium: $0.

fps hold ($0.07B, doctrine)
- Gives up $0.07B in every column against the 10-year at Renton (-0.94 / -1.27 / -0.94).
- Reason: doing less within ε [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].
- What breaks the number: a slip cost above about $1.0B on the +3-year clean-sheet prior (Malave), or an overrun above about 2.1% (Pope). The hold then becomes a saving.

787 Re-engine hold (logged separately as a Board hold, not against the cap)
- The binding reason is the Board's +$1B business-case line. My own ε rule and Malave's worst-column tie-break pick the hold too.
- Known cost: $0.74B given up in S1 and S3, $0.81B saved in S2.
- Weighted: $0.35B at Malave's 25% ($0.43B at 20%, $0.28B at 30%).
- What breaks the number: an A350 Re-engine turns the hold into a saving of $0.81B and closes the Re-engine for good under H3.
- Counted as soft instead, the total would be $0.81B, still inside $2B. The classification changes no decision.

Objective premium: $0. No launch this round moves a scored year: the earliest fps EIS is 2052, and every plan shows one engine source in 2050.
boeing.objective_note:
The company objectives are the company's mission, not on my ranked list. They never change the payoff, and no PV is given up for them this round.

Met:
- repair the balance sheet (2029), and keep it repaired in base and stress at every check year;
- three narrowbody engine makers in the market in 2045 and 2050.

Not met:
- hold the 50/50 split and defend incumbency (worst year 20.0%; 2045 and 2050 at 20.0%);
- dual or triple sources on our narrowbody (the 737 MAX flies CFM only, 1 source in 2040, 2045 and 2050).

No order this round can move a scored year: an fps launched now enters service in 2052 or later, and every plan shows 1 engine source in 2050.

The long-cycle stake is real but unscored: under the lead-edge rule the long-run split is 32-35% for a launch now and 27-30% for a 2050 launch. That goes into the 2050 case as information, not as a reason to waive the Board's +$1B line.

The engine-sourcing requirement is updated to code 7 (CFM plus the Joint Venture, two sources), so the enabler is ready whenever the airplane is.
boeing.predictions:
AIRBUS

frame.situation:
Round 3, decision year 2045. We have launched nothing. We are on today's products: the 737 MAX with a ceiling of 57 a month (684 a year), and the 787.

**Public record**
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, with CFM, P&W and RR on it. Airbus confirmed its Alt plan at the 2035 gate, so A320 lines are kept longer.
- P&W and RR formed the Joint Venture in 2035. GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded into it, and its engine has been ready since 2036.
- CFM's ducted engine has been ready since 2041. The CFM-Embraer partnership has been ready since 2042.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. So H3's second half has not closed the 787 Re-engine.

**Market on Do Nothing (S1 -1.01: narrowbody operating profit -3.64, offset by +2.63 from supply and demand)**
- Preference share has been 20% since 2043.
- Delivered share fell to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45. It returns to 36.3% from 2047, because Airbus's capacity of about 1,200 a year binds and its flexible customers take our free slots.
- MAX deliveries: 458 (2044), 521 (2045), 618 (2046), then 684 from 2047. That is a climb from about 43 to 51.5 to 57 a month, inside today's ceiling. It is not a Rate Increase.
- From 2047, new demand runs above both makers' slots: 1,976 against 684 + 1,200 = 1,884 in 2047, and 2,232 against 1,884 in 2050.
- That is what moved the fps item. It was -1.20 in 2035. Ten years of discounting alone would make that -0.44; it is now +0.07, so about $0.51B of the gain is real.
- The Re-engine's 2.01 in 2035, discounted ten years, is exactly its +0.74 today. Its case has not grown.

**Balance sheet**
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029, in base and stress, through 2060. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year.
- Profit is $0.63B below the game baseline in 2045 and back to baseline by 2050. Allocating the surplus is the Board's call.

**Objectives**
- Balance-sheet lines: all met.
- 50/50 split and incumbency: not met (worst year 20%).
- Three narrowbody engine makers in the market: met.
- Two or more sources on our own narrowbody: not met (the MAX flies CFM only). Every plan shows 1 source in 2050, because the earliest fps EIS is 2052. No launch this round moves any scored year.

**KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. rate_737 is hold only.

**Grid columns**
- S1: rivals hold. S2: Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine. S3: the risk case, covert Airbus Delay Tactics.
- S3 equals S1 on every row. My reading, for Malave to confirm: Delay Tactics move preference, and from 2047 demand exceeds the slots, so they cost us nothing on this board. That makes the slip leg a level test this round, and S2 the worst column on every row.

**Board guidance (it does not bind, but its veto binds after my decision)**
- It would veto:
  - every fps launch, on the business case (best item +0.07 against +$1B);
  - via Embraer, on Rating first and on Malave's buffer;
  - re787: launch. Alone it is +0.74, below +$1B. Beside an fps it is -1.06 or -1.27 in S2, and beside a 7-year fps it overlaps for 5 years.
- It would approve a hold on both and new_site. It takes Renton only with a launch and a MAX bridge plan, and welcomes code 7 at any launch.
- It wants to see:
  - item values in S1, S2 and S3;
  - S3 against Do Nothing (line -3.01);
  - Malave's buffer and 'Fundable when the 777X turns' results;
  - net debt in base and stress;
  - Pope's gates, including the 2045-47 MAX climb, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA;
  - H3's second half confirmed;
  - every premium logged, with the Re-engine hold logged separately;
  - the cost of waiting;
  - no reason that cites Airbus.
- I carry these as Board risks, not red lines.
