cfo.would_change_mind_if:
The orders cannot change: hold is the only legal value in both fields, so no weights and no evidence move them. What would change my numbers or my advice:
(1) Weights. A Boeing launch signal on the public record would move S2 above 0.40: a dated fps, a supply-plan choice, or a sourcing move that names an EIS. A further 'not this year' with the MAX still at 57 would move it down. The row stays negative at any weights.
(2) The S2 gap. A GM year table for S2 that puts the -0.59 in 2038-44 would let me tell the Finance Committee it is a scoring effect on delivered years, not cash at risk. If the gap sits in 2045-56, it is a real preference loss on our volume.
(3) The bridge. A year table for the 2035 S4 projection would let me trace the +2.15 that did not show. Until then I project nothing the brief cannot show year by year.
(4) Ground 3. A Rolls-Royce request for a technology credit in cash beyond equal shares, or in gear or core access. It comes to me as a capital item, and I would veto it.
(5) Ground 4. A draft that claims durability beyond the in-service data, makes a payback claim, or states a Rolls-Royce block or a Boeing date as fact. I would veto it.
(6) Cash. Fleet costs (spares, MRO capacity, a Hot Section shortfall in service) above plan, or block integration cost beyond equal shares. Those return to Finance, and I would reopen the envelope view. The stretch stays in reserve until then.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. One legal row, 'GTF2: hold': -0.14 in S1, -0.73 in S2. S2 is the worst column. My weights are 0.60/0.40: Boeing's delivery share has fallen from 40.1% to 26.6% and its balance sheet is repaired. Expected PV -0.38, negative at any weights; each 0.10 moved to S2 costs $0.06B.

Cash: new R&D in 2045 is $0. GTF2's $2.0B, booked in 2035, covers our $2B Joint Venture share with no fold write-off. The envelope is untouched, the stretch stays in reserve, the dividend is whole and debt stays on its pre-ASR path.

The honest account. In 2035 I booked +0.48. We are at -0.14, and 'capitalise on the GTF' is not met. My first read would be timing. It isn't: the -0.62 is all engine value, a step. Through 2041 we ran at or above plan. From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership took our NGSA share from about 38% to 36.5%: 44 engines a year to 2056. My 2035 grid had no CFM column, and I put the low end in the wrong place. The S4 +2.15 never showed: 2041 came in at 826 engines, the S1 projection exactly.

S2 sits below S1 because the two-airframe rule cuts Airbus's preference while Boeing's P&W slot arrives only in 2055. I book neither.

A derived +0.77, with R&D discounted at 10%, goes to Finance only, never booked.

No veto. Hold and hold. Take the Finance routing out of the public terms; 'never' is the floor.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only legal values in the brief (section 3), so nothing goes to the Board.

gtf2_solo HOLD. GTF2 was launched in 2030 and was due ready in 2036. It folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and its tested configuration is the engine fitted on NGSA. It can no longer be launched, cancelled or relaunched, and it needs no new R&D. Grid row 'GTF2: hold': -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2). I take no view on the weights; that is Neil's.

jv_with_rr HOLD. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and the rules allow a withdraw only before formation, so my 2035 withdraw conditions have lapsed as orders. Both technical conditions still hold, as governance:
(1) the Joint Venture engine is ready by every live EIS: ready 2036, NGSA EIS 2037, S2 fps EIS 2055;
(2) the gear and core stay P&W modules under P&W type data (published term 2). The brief shows no breach.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Proposal: hold, hold. Confirmed.

2. In-service record. The brief and bulletin carry no fleet data: no time on wing, no hot-and-harsh or severe-environment results, no life-limited-part lives, no AOG count and no turn times. The board does not model durability. So I can't tell you the fleet is where it needs to be [PX-0022], and I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. I said that in June 2023, five weeks before the recall [PX-0112][PX-0290].
- The public record shows only that nothing public has happened. No P&W fleet, AOG or quality event appears in any bulletin from 2037 to 2044. P&W's NGSA flow rose from about 8 engines (2037) to about 800 (2044), derived from the public shares (inference). None of that proves durability.
- To the Governance and Public Policy Committee I bring the data as they exist:
(a) time on wing against plan, cooler against hot-and-sandy operators, as I split it in 2023 [PX-0122];
(b) removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage [PX-0116][P-0785];
(c) severe-environment and fleet-leader findings (inference);
(d) every life-limited part's life against full life, with any life-limit reduction [PX-0128];
(e) configuration percentages, AOG count, shop-visit rate, turn times and the pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly [PX-0123][PX-0131].
If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so.

3. Readiness. Confirmed. The engine has been ready since 2036 (launch + 6, carried over at the fold).
- NGSA: code 7, EIS 2037, in service.
- S2: a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055 on code 7, which includes P&W. 2036 is earlier than 2055, a 19-year margin. A 7-year fps (2052) or an Embraer fps (2055) passes too.
- There is no readiness gap anywhere on the board.
- Advice: what we offer Boeing is the standard in service. A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof, and I promise none.

4. Parts, spares and capacity.
Counted flow (brief section 1):
- 816 (2036), 580 (2037, -29%), 639, 668, 694, 826 (2041, +132, +19%, the largest step), 821, 834, 936 (2044, +102, peak, +15% on 2036), 892 (2045), then 876 from 2046 (-6% off peak, flat).
- That is under the 2035 projection: 2044 at 936 against 976 (-4%), and 876 against 920 from 2047 (-5%).

Mix (derived from public shares, inference):
- GTF OE on the A320neo held at about 440-615 a year in 2037-40 and fell to about 136 by 2044.
- The NGSA engine went from about 8 to about 254 (2040), then to about 800 (2044).
- So the 2037-40 dip was a mix shift, not a lull. The window I named in 2035 was narrower than I said, and that's on me.

Gear and core (inference):
- Under our own terms only P&W makes the gear and core, and every NGSA Joint Venture engine is GTF2's tested configuration until a Rolls-Royce block passes its gate. So our gear and core sit in the Rolls-Royce-credited engines too.
- That module flow rose from about 588 (2037) to about 1,736 (2044), roughly three times, while the counted flow rose 61%. It runs at about 1,750 a year from 2046 (876 each).
- The pacing parts and spares for the gear and core must be sized to that, not to 876.
- The brief has no parts count, so I can't show that capacity covered the climb. I fall short on evidence, and I say so [PX-0066].

Shops:
- The GTF fleet built since 2026 is about 12,100 engines (816 a year for 2026-36, plus about 3,126 for 2037-44, derived). It is ageing into heavy visits.
- The NGSA fleet is about 3,600-3,800 engines by end-2045 and about 8,000 by 2050 (derived).
- I have no time-on-wing data to date the NGSA engine's first shop-visit wave, and I won't guess.

Allocation:
- Fleet spares stay ahead of OE and block hardware when they compete for parts [PX-0080][PX-0123].
- From about 2046 the A320neo GTF OE is gone, so the contest is NGSA OE against two fleets in the shops.
- We agree OE allocation with Airbus jointly [PX-0099] and tell them early where we fall short [PX-0066].
- We fix forward. The Hot Section kit goes into GTF shop visits at value [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. Any NGSA durability fix enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.

5. The Rolls-Royce block gate, held to the Advantage rule.
(a) Configuration control. GTF2's tested configuration stays the type standard. Any Rolls-Royce module change is a new block under a joint configuration board, with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core.
(b) Spares. No intermix in shop visits until the block is certified and its own spares are stocked. GTF2-standard spares are never drawn down for block hardware.
(c) Testing. At least Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme [PX-0084]) at representative severe-environment, hot-and-sandy conditions [PX-0128][PX-0122]. Endurance testing must show time on wing no worse than the fitted standard, with interface load tests on our gear and core.
(d) Full life. Every Rolls-Royce life-limited part has full life at entry into service [PX-0128].
(e) Production and support. Rolls-Royce parts capacity is qualified before rate, because powder metal came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. Its partner-shop support is in place before entry into service.
(f) The route. The data, not a plan, go to the committee. The block enters service only after the committee clears it. No date is given, and if the data are late, the block waits.

6. Joint Venture governance. Published terms 1 and 2: each partner owns its modules, a joint integration and test team works the interfaces (the team mirrors the architecture [P-1240]), and the gear and core are P&W modules under P&W type data, with no licence, data access or transfer [P-1233]. The brief shows no breach. I can't audit the Joint Venture's internals from it.

Rolls-Royce's two statements, 'the folded UltraFan keeps its own test programme through to entry into service' and its separate UltraFan offer to Boeing, read two ways:
- as Rolls-Royce modules entering as a later block through our gate; or
- as a separate narrowbody engine, named by product and with its own test programme, kept alive under the Joint Venture label.
On the board, UltraFan NB folded and Rolls-Royce's narrowbody engine is the Joint Venture engine. Off the board, I can't tell, and we state no Rolls-Royce intention as fact.
- The technical tell: a block that brings its own gear or core is not a block on our engine. That would be the alignment break [P-1875] and a Board-level risk.
- What settles it: Rolls-Royce confirms in writing that UltraFan content enters only as a block on the Joint Venture engine, through the joint team and our gate, and that any Boeing offer is the Joint Venture engine.

7. Engineering load (advice; no strain charge on this board).
- Fleet support: about 12,100 GTF engines and the growing NGSA fleet.
- Block integration: interface work only. Rolls-Royce's modules are Rolls-Royce's.
- The Boeing offer: the in-service standard, with no work until a launch.
None of it pulls from fleet support if the integration team is staffed separately. A Boeing-specific block would be a new development: one at a time, after the fleet, and to Finance.

8. Veto check: no veto.
- Ground 1: no Rolls-Royce block, no EIS date and no durability claim appears in the orders or in your draft.
- Ground 2: no launch or new commitment is ordered, and the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem.
Watch items are listed under vetoes.

9. Disclosure check: it passes. No durability is claimed beyond the data, no EIS date is given, the Boeing line is a condition, and the GTF2 lines are retired. Three edits:
(a) 'CFM has a new engine in service': the record says 'ready since 2041'. Say 'ready' or 'a new engine'.
(b) 'Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block' should read 'Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block', so that it reads as our term and not as Rolls-Royce's intention.
(c) Keep 'we are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity'. Don't upgrade it to 'sized' until I can show the gear-and-core count.
Counsel reviews the GTF paragraph.

My record is one event, June 2023, and it is silent on Joint Ventures. Items 5 to 7 are seat doctrine and inference.

other_moves.detail:
The fleet comes before any new hardware [PX-0080][PX-0084].
- The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100].
- Fleet spares and MRO material are allocated ahead of NGSA OE and ahead of any Joint Venture block hardware when they compete for the same parts.
- We fix forward through shop-visit upgrades. Any durability fix for the NGSA engine enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.

No date is given for any ramp or recovery. The move has no effect on the game board.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governed to its published terms; 'never' restated as the public floor
other_moves.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms we published in 2035, restated with one change: the Finance routing comes out of the public text.
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233].
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

other_moves.move: Standing offer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts

This answers Boeing's standing invitation to all three engine makers. We offer the Joint Venture engine, which has been ready since 2036, in the standard now in service. It is offered on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100], and the same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer.
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing either way.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We will report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support, the GTF and the new engine together.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block. It would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr hold. Both are the only legal values (brief section 3), and both are the default, so nothing goes to the Board. premium_b is 0 and overrides is empty.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP:

(1) Start from Eddy's proposal. He proposes hold and hold, and Mitchill recommends the same.

(2) Strike any plan that fails a binding veto. None does.
- Mitchill: ground 1 (dividend and debt) is not engaged at $0 of new R&D. Ground 2 (unselected engine) is not applicable, because no live GTF2 exists and the Joint Venture engine is selected and fitted on NGSA. Ground 3 (terms) passes. Ground 4 (upside) passes.
- Mitchill's two conditional vetoes, on a partner credit beyond equal shares and on overclaiming in the disclosure, are not engaged. I took his wording fixes into the statement: 'no new engine development spending'; 'CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041'; 'any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block'.
- Eddy: both grounds pass. The engine has been ready since 2036, against NGSA's 2037 and S2's 2055, and no block, date or durability claim appears. His watch item is not triggered. I took his edits: 'Under the Joint Venture's terms'; 'sizing', not 'sized'.

(3) Safety and durability set the constraint [PX-0035][PX-0073]. No Rolls-Royce block enters service before its own proof and full-life parts reach the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and GTF2's tested configuration stays the fitted standard until then. Eddy has no fleet data to show, so the disclosure claims no durability for the NGSA engine. It says we will report it as the data show it.

(4) Optimise. There is one row: 'GTF2: hold', -0.14 (S1) / -0.73 (S2). It is the best grid plan in both columns because it is the only one.

(5) Tie-breaks. 'The fleet beats a new engine' governs the other moves. 'Miss a cycle' does not apply: the Joint Venture engine is already ready for any code that includes us, and S2 is code 7. A rival's discount moves nothing.

WEIGHTS: S1 0.60, S2 0.40. I move from my framing 0.65/0.35 to Mitchill's and the Board's 0.40.
- For S2: Boeing's NB delivery share fell from 40.1% to 26.6%, its balance sheet is repaired, and its sourcing move names code 7. Those are lead indicators.
- My own incrementalism on a rival's timing [PX-0093] pulls me low, and Mitchill books downside early.
- Expected PV: 0.6 x -0.14 + 0.4 x -0.73 = -0.376, reported as -0.38. Worst column: S2, -0.73.
- The row is negative at any weights, and nothing on the orders turns on them.
- I say nothing on Boeing's dates [PX-0062], and nothing we do is aimed at its timing either way.

THE HONEST ACCOUNT (Mitchill's numbers; I trust his cash over my dates):
- The booked -0.14 is engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00, charged undiscounted.
- The -0.62 since 2035 is all engine value, a step, not timing. Through 2041 we ran at or above plan. From 2042, CFM's ducted engine and its Embraer partnership took about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half from us. That is about 44 engines a year: 920 became 876. The attribution is derived inference from public tables.
- Our 2035 grid had no CFM column. The +2.15 that S4 projected never showed.
- S2 is -0.59 below S1 because the two-airframe share rule cuts Airbus's preference while the MAX stays on CFM, and the fps's P&W slot enters service only in 2055, against an NB count that ends in 2056. The fps volume beyond 2056 is real in 'miss a cycle' terms [PX-0071], but it is RTX-wide in my record, inferred here, and not booked.
- The derived WACC-discounted figure (about +0.77) goes to Finance only. It is never booked and never public.

DISCLOSURE: the GTF2 'due ready 2036 ... carrying it through' lines are retired as history. 'Responsible bets with responsible paybacks' [PX-0010] is dropped, because -0.14 does not support it. The Boeing line is a condition, not a forecast. 'Never' is the public floor on technology credit, and the Finance routing moves to the private record. Counsel reviews the GTF paragraph.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: my record is Low on the Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. Its governance, the block gate and the alignment request follow company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875], Eddy's seat doctrine and Mitchill's cash test. I defer to Eddy on readiness, parts and capacity.

BIASES WATCHED:
- Operating-date optimism: no block, ramp or recovery date is given.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2's configuration stays the standard only until Rolls-Royce's proof is in, not as pride.
- Incrementalism on Boeing: I corrected toward Mitchill's 0.40.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily, as the team rule and my profile direct: I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- Adopted: his weights (0.60/0.40), the expected PV of -0.38 and S2 as the worst column, the envelope check ($0 new R&D, GTF2's $2.0B covering our $2B share, no fold write-off), and the dividend and debt confirmation.
- His NPV bridge goes to the Finance Committee as written. The -0.62 is a step from CFM's moves from 2042, not timing. The S4 +2.15 never showed. The end-state 23.3% is derived.
- His candour that the 2035 grid had no CFM column, and that the low end was put in the wrong place, is the account I own.
- His explanation of S2 corrects mine on two points: Airbus's free slots, and the possibility that part of the gap sits in delivered years.
- His wording fixes are all taken, and his advice on term (3) is taken: 'never' stays public, the routing goes private.
- His two conditional vetoes (ground 3 on any partner credit beyond equal shares, ground 4 on any overclaim) are respected and not engaged.
- The derived +0.77 stays labelled, for Finance only.
- His 'fail' on the programme return against a buyback is reported, not hidden. No order can change it.

- The most important line in either memo is his: the brief carries no fleet data, so we claim no durability for the NGSA engine. He will not say there is no surprise coming, having said that five weeks before the recall. That sets the disclosure.
- His derived point that every Joint Venture engine carries our gear and core, about 1,750 modules a year, goes into the fleet move and the risk register. That flow, not 876, is what the pacing parts must be sized to.

other_moves.move: Capital allocation frame
other_moves.detail: Cash from the Trent and Joint Venture fleets goes first to the balance sheet, then to a 30-40% dividend payout, then to investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0242, RX-0213, RX-0215, RX-0261].

other_moves.move: Rolls-Royce-module durability gates reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round
other_moves.detail: Watson reports the gates with no date: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. Our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service; no pacing bent to any airframer's ramp; no concession to P&W or any airframer. P&W's GTF hot-and-sandy time-on-wing record is the watch item. If a gate fails, the block waits and we tell Airbus and P&W early [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476, R-0970].

other_moves.move: Widebody watch for 2050
other_moves.detail: If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, the ExCo brings one row, A350 first, on the 2050 grid with its item value, worst column against its own bill and the $5B strain shown. Bars (team doctrine, inference): the upgrade needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB needs a Re-engine on the record and at least +$4B weighted before the strain, so its shortfall sits inside the $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column. Otherwise the core is protected through time on wing.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields. ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold. None of these is a Board item. It is my proposal, both memos recommend it, and nothing struck it.

THE QUESTION, IN CASH AND QUALITY OF EARNINGS [RX-0054]. We made the narrowbody bet, paid for it, and it is earning. The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our narrowbody share is 25.1% in 2045 and 23.3% from 2047: 872 engines this year, 876 a year after that. Narrowbody development money ended at $5.71B, all booked in 2035: our $4B share plus a $1.71B write-off. Today's ΔPV is +9.61 (engine value +15.32, R&D -4.00, write-off -1.71). Following Watson's caution, I credit the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year. This round is about protecting those earnings and the widebody franchise, not adding activity.

GRID, COLUMN BY COLUMN. Item value is the row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'.
- Hold row 'UltraFan NB: hold': +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86 (S1-S4). Best in every column. Worst column +9.61.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade': row +3.13 / +3.14 / +3.13 / +3.40. Item -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46. With the $5B strain added back, -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46. Worst column -6.48 against its own $2B bill. Widebody would go from 55.2% to 60.0% in 2050, but 55.2% already clears the line. McCabe puts the extra engines at about +$0.52B of PV against a $2B bill.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB': row +0.61 / +0.62 / +1.33 / +1.84. Item -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02. With the strain added back, -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02. Worst column -9.00 against its own $4B bill. Widebody stays at 55.2% in every column, because it would be ready in 2051, a year after any Re-engine launched now.
- The two widebody items are exclusive, so there is no joint row. Both narrowbody fields are hold only.

WEIGHTS. There is no selection to weigh. The columns are rivals' moves, so P is 0.1 for 'nothing on the record' (inference). Sets (calculation in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-sd/work/r3_decide_calc.py):
- B, the Board's illustrative set, confirmed by McCabe: 0.70 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05. Hold +9.624; upgrade item -6.479 (-1.479 before strain); UltraFan WB item -8.879 (-3.879).
- C/M, my read and McCabe's: 0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05. Same votes; hold +9.623.
- U, uniform: hold +9.675; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
- R, Re-engine-heavy: 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.25. Hold +9.674; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
No set changes any vote. Both widebody items lose in every column, even before the strain.

TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing declined a 787 Re-engine. That fails UltraFan WB outright.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: the upgrade fails on the business model (it loses before the strain, and the strain is anti-synergy). UltraFan WB fails on the market and the business model.
- Profitable or not at all [RX-0058]: neither item clears zero.
- Premium cap: the upgrade shortfall (about $6.5B) is more than double the $3B cap. UltraFan WB's ($8.6-8.9B) is far over the $1B sub-cap.
- Reasonable worst case: both items lose more than their own bill in every column.
- Widebody franchise [R-1574]: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 on every held row. The 2.8 pp step in 2042 is the GEnx upgrade. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: Do Nothing commits no new programme money. For the record, capex for either item would be about $0.67B a year (£0.49-0.50bn), plus $5B of strain (about £3.7bn), roughly a year of FY2026 free cash flow guidance.
- My pull toward the 787 ('Why not?' [RX-0117], 'regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]) is real. The grid says why not. The answer is time on wing, not a programme weighed down by a $5B strain.

VETO CHECKS.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature, binding, on t1000_upgrade launch and ultrafan_wb launch. Neither is ordered, so nothing needs revising. Her balance-sheet vetoes are not triggered: no equity, no borrowing, no change in leverage. A fall in the brief's ΔPV is not a trigger.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto on the proposed orders. Maturity is not compressed: the Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2. His conditional veto covers the final statement, the other moves and this rationale. I have written them to his tests: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block or Rolls-Royce content anywhere; nothing that counts on our modules entering service by a year or being on the fps at its EIS; partner shops are ours, with P&W's shops adding capacity only after, never instead; the Boeing answer is Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan, with support in place before entry into service; no fps or Re-engine dates go public.

RED-LINE FLAGS.
- McCabe flagged that an ultrafan_wb launch would break the company rule of no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it. Struck: not ordered.
- The upgrade breaks no overlap red line on the board, since no UltraFan is in development. It is struck on money grounds alone.
- No cancel is available, and nothing orphaned stands: the Joint Venture flies on NGSA [RX-0051].
- overrides is empty.

OBJECTIVES, PLAINLY.
- Narrowbody entry: met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Widebody dominance: met (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the line).
- Bounded narrowbody risk (at most $4B): not met, locked at $5.71B (the Solo's 2030-2035 spend, folded into the Joint Venture). No order this round moves it. We accepted that because an airframe selected us.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0 strain, and kept only by holding both widebody items. I will not trade it for a widebody programme that pays on no column.

ROUND-2 BOARD ITEMS: closed or carried; see board_response.

DOCTRINE, NOT RECORD. The column weights, the 2050 widebody bars (upgrade +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB a Re-engine on the record and +$4B weighted before the strain) and the worst-case rule are team doctrine (inference). On the UltraFan WB bar I take McCabe's +$4B over the Board's +$3B: only +$4B keeps the shortfall inside the Board's own $1B sub-cap.

"We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically." [RX-0058]

She confirms the capital frame and that no balance-sheet trigger is in play. On S2 she shows there is nothing to concede (+$0.01B, about £7m). I take her 2050 bar for UltraFan WB (+$4B weighted before the strain) over the Board's +$3B, because only hers keeps the shortfall inside the $1B sub-cap. Her flag that an UltraFan WB launch would break the no-programme-to-fly-it rule is noted and struck, since it is not ordered.
memo_weighing.ops: Weighed heavily on readiness, support and statement discipline, and adopted in full. Watson concurs with Do Nothing and invokes no Civil veto on the orders. The Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2, not compressed, and is in service on NGSA with no fleet event on the record. P&W's GTF time on wing in hot and sandy conditions is our watch item, and our module proof covers hot and harsh conditions. I wrote the statement, the other moves and the rationale to his conditional veto: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block; nothing that counts on our modules being in service by a year or on the fps at its EIS; partner shops ours, P&W's adding capacity after, never instead; the Boeing answer is our part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan. I kept the fps planning gates internal. His capacity read (narrowbody load at 84% of what we sized for in round 2) is advice and holds. His view that the upgrade would compete for the same engineers as our module proof supports the hold.

2045 round, private:

would_veto:
`t1000_upgrade: launch`.
- Reasonable worst case: the item value (row 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46. Every column is below its -$2B bill, because the $5B strain is stacked on it.

- Without the strain it is still -1.48. The rise to 60.0% widebody share in 2050 does not pay for the upgrade's $2B.
- The overlap rule is not the ground on the grid: the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, so no UltraFan is in development. The money ground stands on its own.
- Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`ultrafan_wb: launch`.
- Airframe on the record: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing's last statement declined a 787 Re-engine.
- Reasonable worst case: the item value (row 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02, beyond its -$4B bill in every column.

Any `launch` without McCabe's co-signature (as defined in our process), with a binding Civil veto still standing, or with a non-empty `overrides`. These are governance grounds, and they apply on top of the money grounds above.
- Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

recommendations.text:
Hold both widebody items, and say why in plain numbers in `rationale`. With the Joint Venture on the record, ready and not cancellable, any widebody programme carries its bill plus the $5B strain for good.
- This round the upgrade is -6.48 and UltraFan WB is -8.02 to -9.00. Before the strain they are -1.48 and -3.02 to -4.00.

tests.threshold: A Re-engine must be on the public record. The row must also beat hold, or the gap must be declared as a premium within $3B (Board sub-cap for UltraFan WB: $1B) (inference).
tests.numbers:
Row 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' (+0.61 / +0.62 / +1.33 / +1.84) minus hold gives -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02.
- Expected gain: -8.879 on B and on M/C; -8.575 on U and R.
- Before the strain: -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02, or -3.88 on B and -3.58 on U.
No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing declined one. Widebody share stays at 55.2% in 2050 in every column, because UltraFan WB is not ready until 2051. The shortfall of about $8.6-8.9B is far over the $1B sub-cap.

tests.name: Hurdle: Do Nothing on all four fields
tests.threshold: The plan must be the PV-best row inside the red lines. No launch means there is nothing to co-sign.
tests.numbers: Hold row: +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86, the best row in every column. Item value 0.00. It is not a Board item. ΔPV of +9.61 reconciles to engine value +15.32, less R&D of 4.00 (our Joint Venture share), less the 1.71 write-off.

tests.name: Unselected downside / worst column against own bill
tests.threshold: State the worst column of every row. No item may lose more than its own bill in any plausible column.
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing (recommended): worst column +9.61 (S1, S3). No new bill, so it passes.
- Trent 1000 upgrade: worst -6.48 (S1-S3) against a $2B bill, 3.2 times the bill. It fails.
- UltraFan WB: worst -9.00 (S1, S2) against a $4B bill, 2.25 times the bill. It fails.
In both cases the $5B strain is stacked on the item, and neither stays within its own bill even before the strain in S1 (UltraFan WB -4.00 against $4B, at the limit). The result reads 'fail' for the two rejected items only.

tests.name: Capex a year in GBP (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: For information only; my evidence sets no threshold.
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: no new programme money. Narrowbody development spend has ended at $5.71B: our $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B write-off, all booked in 2035 (the brief's year table shows 5.7 in 2035 and nothing after).
- Upgrade: $2B over 3 years, about $0.67B a year, or £0.49-0.50bn a year at 1.36-1.34 $/£. That is 13-14% of FY2026 FCF guidance (£3.6-3.8bn), the latest on the record.
- UltraFan WB: $4B over 6 years, the same £0.49-0.50bn a year.
- Either item adds the one-off $5B strain, about £3.68-3.73bn, which is roughly 97-104% of a full year's FY2026 FCF guidance (inference).

tests.name: Flat R&D envelope and strain (advice)
tests.threshold: Report any overlap and the $5B strain, which the grid already includes (do not deduct it again). New money is redeployed, not added (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: $0 strain in every column (objective table, row 'UltraFan NB: hold').
- Either widebody item: $5B in every column, for good. The Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled, and the upgrade would be ready in 2048, before the 2050 round, so its strain could never be removed.
- Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing work (HP turbine blades, life-limited part extensions) is redeployed inside a broadly flat envelope, not added.
- Red lines: no UltraFan is in development, so the overlap red line does not bite.

tests.name: Balance sheet (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: No equity raise. No new borrowing to rebuild the balance sheet. Leverage up to about 1-1.5x only for the right opportunity. Never lever up for buybacks.

tests.name: Joint Venture cost against Solo
tests.threshold: Read against hold. The fold write-off and share equalisation are already in the grid and are not deducted again (inference).
tests.numbers:
The Joint Venture formed in 2035. Our narrowbody money is $5.71B ($4B share plus $1.71B written off) against the Solo's $8B: $2.29B saved, about £1.68-1.71bn. That is what my round-2 memo set out, and it was delivered.
The write-off and the equal-share rule are inside the hold row (+9.61). The round-2 Board item to price the equalisation at a 2045 formation is closed by the 2035 formation.
Observed 2044: P&W 27.1% against RR 23.2% of all narrowbody engines. On the rules, the gap is P&W's legacy A320neo slot (CFM 60% / P&W 40%), not the Joint Venture split (inference).

tests.name: Cancel write-off
tests.threshold: Bill x years elapsed / development years. Book the write-off arithmetic, not the sunk cost.
tests.numbers:
No cancel is available this round: the Solo folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture is ready and cannot be cancelled.
For the record, the exit costs of the widebody items:
- UltraFan WB launched now and cancelled in 2050 would write off $4B x 5/6 = $3.33B, with nothing to show for it.
- The upgrade would be ready in 2048, so it could not be cancelled, and its $5B strain would be locked in.

tests.name: Short payback first
tests.threshold: State when each order starts to earn. The brief gives no payback years (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: the Joint Venture engine has earned on NGSA since 2037. Our narrowbody engines run at 872 in 2045 and 876 a year from 2046, and widebody at 188 a year.
- Upgrade: counts from 2048.
- UltraFan WB: ready in 2051, and it counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. None is on the record.

tests.name: Premium (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Price every doctrine or objective premium in $B. Above $3B a round, the PV-best order applies. UltraFan WB is capped at $1B.

tests.name: Objectives, reported plainly (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: The objective metrics from the brief, section 2. These are not hard rules.
tests.numbers:
- Narrowbody entry: met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Widebody: met (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the line).
- Bounded risk: not met. It is locked at $5.71B, both narrowbody fields are hold-only, and no order moves it.
- Never starved: met at $0, and kept only by holding both widebody items.

tests.name: Boeing answer, standard terms (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: No concession to buy share. Win-win terms, through the Investment Committee.
tests.numbers: S2 lifts the hold row by $0.01B (+9.62 against +9.61), about £7m. Any concession worth more than that destroys value, and £7m is below the £25m joint sign-off line. Nothing is worth conceding. The renewed offer stays on standard terms, with no launch discount and durability proven before entry into service as a condition. A durability condition is not a price.

tests.name: 2050 look-ahead: the widebody bar (CEO ask 9)
tests.threshold: An item must lose no more than its own bill in any plausible column, and its shortfall must sit within the premium cap ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB) (inference).
tests.numbers:
Upgrade (counts 2053-2061):
- It needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column, which means about $5B of PV from the extra engines.
- Today it shows about $0.52B over 14 counted years, and a 2050 launch counts only 9.
UltraFan WB (ready 2056, counts to 2061):
- It needs a Re-engine on the record and at least +$4B weighted before the strain, which means about $8B of PV.
- Today's S4 gives under $1B.
- The Board's '+$3B weighted' would leave a $2B shortfall, above its own $1B sub-cap.
I expect hold again in 2050 unless a Re-engine moves the columns (inference).

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch
vetoes.ground:
It fails the hurdle and the worst-case test.
- It never beats hold: -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46, and -6.48 on any weights.
- Its worst column, -6.48, is 3.2 times its own $2B bill, because the $5B strain is stacked on it and would be locked in for good (the upgrade is ready in 2048).
- Before the strain it is still -1.48.
- The premium of about $6.5B is more than double the $3B cap.
I withhold my co-signature, and the order stays hold. The overlap red line does not bite, because the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch
vetoes.ground:
It fails the hurdle and the worst-case test.
- Expected gain: -8.88 on B and -8.58 uniform.
- Its worst column, -9.00, is 2.25 times its own $4B bill.
- Before the strain it is -3.02 to -4.00.
- The shortfall is far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap.
I withhold my co-signature, and the order stays hold. Separately, no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, so a launch would also break the company hard rule 'no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it'. I flag that breach for the CEO; it is not my ground.

vetoes.plan: Balance-sheet vetoes (equity raise, leverage above about 1.5x, levering up for buybacks)
vetoes.ground: Not triggered. Do Nothing commits no new programme cash: no equity, no borrowing, no change in leverage. A fall in the brief's ΔPV is not a trigger.

vetoes.plan: Any concession or launch discount to win the Boeing fps or widebody share (an other move; none is proposed)
vetoes.ground: This is a standing condition on my support, not a veto of the CEO's proposal. S2 is worth $0.01B (about £7m) to the hold row, so there is nothing to concede. If a concession appears in the other moves, I withhold my support.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Delivered numbers and an announced customer would change my view.
- A Re-engine on the record: if a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, I re-test one widebody row, A350 first, on that round's grid. The upgrade would need at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column. UltraFan WB would need +$4B weighted before the strain to sit within its $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column.
- A corrected grid: if the CEO's final orders or a corrected grid show any widebody row above hold in any column, I re-run the hurdle on it.
- Trent durability: if Watson reports a Trent 1000 or Trent 7000 time-on-wing problem, I fund it inside the flat envelope. It becomes a programme only if a priced row clears the bar.
- A Boeing fps launch on code 7 brings a second airframe on the same engine at no new spend. It changes no order.
- A Civil veto from Watson against the final orders or the statement is his ground. I would say so, and the orders stay at hold.
- Weights: none of my votes turns on them.
cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then the balance sheet. This round is about protecting the cash we have built.

Do Nothing on all four fields is the best row in every column: +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86. That is +9.62 on weights B, which I confirm, and on my own read; +9.68 uniform. It commits no new programme money. Narrowbody development spend ended at $5.71B: our $4B Joint Venture share and $1.71B written off, all booked in 2035. In 2035 we said formation would save about £1.7bn against the Solo. It did.

I withhold my co-signature on both widebody launches, and that binds. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.48 on any weights, worst -6.48 against a $2B bill, and still -1.48 before the strain. UltraFan WB is -8.88 on B, worst -9.00 against a $4B bill, and no Re-engine is on the record. Either one adds the $5B strain for good: about £3.7bn, roughly a year of today's free cash flow guidance. No weighting changes either vote.

S2 is worth $0.01B to us, about £7m, so there is nothing to concede for it.

No balance-sheet trigger is in play.

For 2050, the upgrade would need at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column. UltraFan WB would need a Re-engine on the record and +$4B weighted. Neither is in sight.

My record is silent on engine-launch economics, so these bars are team doctrine. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS (Joint Venture engine on NGSA)
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or at the earlier date the bulletin shows for a folded programme, no later than the EIS of the airframe that selects it. Zero margin passes with a note. A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Formed 2035. Ready 2036 on the bulletin. It took the schedule of the folded GTF2 Solo: 2030 + 6 = 2036, P&W's full six years, not compressed. Formation + 6 alone would be 2041, and our folded UltraFan NB would have been 2037 (2030 + 7). NGSA launched 2030 on code 7, EIS 2037: one year of margin. In service since 2037.

In-service record, brief §1:
- RR narrowbody share: 0.3% (2037), 1.0% (2038), 3.2% (2039), 9.7% (2040), 14.3% (2041), 19.4% (2042), 22.2% (2043), 23.2% (2044), 25.1% (2045), 24.1% (2046), 23.3% from 2047.
- Engines: 7, 23, 80, 254, 423, 583, 700, 802, 872 (2045), then 876 a year.
- Cumulative: 3,744 by 2045 and 8,124 by 2050.

Fleet: the bulletin and the brief report no durability, time-on-wing or quality event on the Joint Venture engine. At its 2035 gate Airbus found 'no supply crunch, engine slip or quality event'. The board does not report time on wing, so I have no first-hand fleet data and claim none.

Watch item (public bulletin): P&W's own account of GTF shortfalls (a powder-metal process issue, shop capacity, shorter time on wing in hot and sandy conditions). Under P&W's terms it supports its own modules. Our proof for the Rolls-Royce modules must cover hot and harsh conditions (inference).

tests.name: Ready by EIS (any fps launched this round)
tests.threshold: The engine must be ready by the fps EIS: launch + 7 (launch_7yr) or launch + 10 (launch_10yr, launch_via_embraer).
tests.numbers:
Joint Venture engine ready 2036. A 2045 fps on launch_7yr has EIS 2052 (+16). On launch_10yr or via Embraer it has EIS 2055 (+19). S2 (10-year, code 5): RR is fitted through the Joint Venture engine, and the hold row gains only +0.01 (+9.62 against +9.61), because a 2055 EIS barely counts by 2056.

These fps dates are internal planning dates only and never go public. The Boeing answer must not imply any date for the Rolls-Royce-module block, nor that our modules will be on the fps by its EIS. It must not offer a Solo UltraFan NB: that programme folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 (inference).

tests.name: Ready by EIS (UltraFan WB, if launched: tested to reject)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. It must be ready by that Re-engine's EIS (launch + 5). A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: Launched 2045, ready 2051. S1 and S2: no Re-engine, so no airframe to meet. S3 and S4: a 787 Re-engine (and an A350 Re-engine) launched 2045 enters service in 2050, so UltraFan WB misses it by one year. That is why the brief keeps widebody share at 55.2% in 2050 in every column. At most 2051-2061 counts. Because 6 > 5, UltraFan WB meets a Re-engine only if it is launched at least a year before that Re-engine, which in practice means a round earlier (arithmetic, inference). The fail is advice, not a veto. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement, public other move or rationale may disclose or count on an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + development years. That means formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the bulletin's 2036 for the folded programme), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, and no date at all for the Rolls-Royce-module block, which its own durability proof gates.
tests.numbers:
CEO's draft statement: 'Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it.' It says nothing on NGSA's rates, fps dates or Re-engine dates, and it retires the round-2 'no earlier than 2037' without putting a new date in its place. The draft public other moves (Trent time on wing, the partner-shop plan, the Boeing answer, standard terms) carry no dates.

The only engine dates on the public record are the bulletin's: the Joint Venture engine ready 2036, NGSA EIS 2037. The draft repeats neither, and neither is early.

Rationale caution: credit the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the board's equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year. I re-check the final text at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a partner-shop support plan must be live before any narrowbody EIS: for the NGSA fleet, before any Rolls-Royce-module block enters service, and before any fps EIS (inference).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody programme (the Joint Venture) beside a widebody programme (Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB) costs a one-off $5B of strain. Red lines: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development; no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers:
Do Nothing: $0 strain in all four columns (brief objective table).

Trent 1000 upgrade: $5B in every column. Item value -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46; before the strain -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46.

UltraFan WB: $5B in every column. Item value -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02; before the strain -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02.

The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and cannot be cancelled, so the strain comes from both programmes being on the record ('for good'), not from overlap years. Only cancelling the widebody item before it is ready would remove it: before 2048 for the upgrade, before 2051 for UltraFan WB.

Red lines on the board record: the upgrade-while-in-development rule does not bite, because no UltraFan is in development (the Solo folded in 2035 and the Joint Venture engine is ready). The NB Solo rule is not applicable. Operationally, the Rolls-Royce-module block's durability proof draws on the same engineers, and that is the load the strain prices (inference).

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief. The board sets no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable; a narrowbody ramp needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers:
Narrowbody: 872 engines in 2045 and 876 a year from 2046. Widebody: 188 a year from 2042. Total about 1,064 a year from 2046, against 197 today and my midterm widebody OE ramp of 300-350.

The narrowbody load is 84% of the about 1,040 a year we sized for in round 2, so it holds with margin. The brief reports no constraint.

Under P&W's terms P&W makes the gear and the core, so the gearbox-sizing constraint now sits on its module (inference). Castings and forgings for our modules go to high-performing suppliers (GBP 685M of GBP 2.5B in 2023).

For widebody shop-visit load I use my figure, 1,100-1,200 a year, not McCabe's 1,400-1,500 definition. The narrowbody shop-visit wave goes through partner shops.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
Every held row, every column: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045), 55.2% (2050). The low point is 55.2%, 5.2 pp above the line, and the 2.8 pp step in 2042 is the GEnx upgrade.

The upgrade would count from 2048 (2045 + 3) and give 60.0% in 2050. That is not needed, and it is -1.48 before the strain. UltraFan WB leaves 55.2% in every column.

There is no Trent 1000 or Trent 7000 durability reason for a programme: the board reports no time-on-wing event. The answer to GEnx is time on wing inside the flat envelope: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000, life-limited part extensions, and the at-least-40% time-on-wing aim.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: UltraFan technology feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values never adjusted.
tests.numbers: UltraFan and the Rolls-Royce-module durability work keep feeding Trent time on wing. This is not priced, and the grid is not adjusted. Holding both widebody items does not stop the Trent fleet work inside the envelope.

vetoes.plan: CEO's proposal: Do Nothing on all four fields (ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold), with the draft statement and the draft other moves
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. I checked all three Civil grounds.
(a) Maturity: not compressed. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 at P&W's full six years and has been in service on NGSA since 2037. The Rolls-Royce modules keep their own test programme through to EIS.
(b) Early date: the draft gives no date for the Rolls-Royce block and none on NGSA, the fps or any Re-engine.
(c) Support: the partner-shop plan is live and ours before any Rolls-Royce block enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe.
No test fails on the proposed orders.

vetoes.plan: Final statement, public other moves and rationale (re-checked at step 4)
vetoes.ground:
Conditional. I invoke the Civil veto if any of these appears:
(a) Any date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce-module block or Rolls-Royce content on any airframe, or any date in the Boeing answer.
(b) Anything that counts on our modules entering service by a given year, or on Rolls-Royce content being on the fps at its EIS. The same applies to a design change counted on before its own durability proof.
(c) Any text in which P&W's shops replace our partner-shop plan before a Rolls-Royce block enters service, or a Boeing answer without support in place before EIS.
If invoked, the team rule makes the veto binding: the CEO revises once, within it. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. On the board it breaks no red line: no UltraFan is in development, since the Solo folded in 2035 and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It adds $5B of strain for good. Item value -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46 against a $2B bill; -1.48 before the strain. Operationally it competes with the Rolls-Royce-module block's durability proof for the same engineers. Advice to hold; the money ground belongs to McCabe and the Board.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. Ready by EIS fails (advice): ready 2051 (2045 + 6), against 2050 for any Re-engine launched this round, and no Re-engine is on the record. It adds $5B of strain for good. Item value -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02; -3.02 to -4.00 before the strain. The CEO's red line (no UltraFan WB without a Re-engine on the record) and the Board's would-veto apply. Advice to hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
(1) A Rolls-Royce-module gate fails, or a fleet durability or time-on-wing event hits the Joint Venture engine on NGSA. Our block then waits, we tell Airbus and P&W early, and testing never bends to a ramp [R-0970].
(2) The final statement, other moves or rationale carries a date for our block, counts on our modules in service by a year (including on the fps), or lets P&W's shops stand in for our partner-shop plan before our block enters service. That is a binding Civil veto.
(3) A 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin. I re-test one row, A350 first. UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056 and counts only once a Re-engine is in service; the upgrade launched in 2050 counts from 2053. Each still carries the $5B strain for good.
(4) Trent 1000 or 7000 durability that the in-envelope work (HP turbine blades, life-limited part extensions) cannot hold, or widebody share heading toward 50% on a further GEnx move. That gives the upgrade a durability case to bring as a row, still against its $2B bill plus the strain.
(5) Supplier or partner-shop capacity that falls short of about 876 narrowbody and 188 widebody engines a year, or of the narrowbody shop-visit wave from a fleet of 8,124 by 2050.
(6) Named airline commitments for the Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce content [RX-0297].
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: Civil tests, 2045. Do Nothing on all four fields. I concur.

Readiness. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, P&W's full six years from GTF2's 2030 launch, not compressed. NGSA entered service in 2037: one year of margin. Our narrowbody engines: 7 in 2037, 872 this year, 876 a year from 2046. The bulletin shows no fleet durability event. P&W's GTF lesson, time on wing in hot and sandy conditions, is our watch item.

Our block. Rolls-Royce modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. No date. No pacing bent to any ramp. No concession. I report the gates to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round.

Support. The partner-shop plan stays live and ours, sized for a second airframe before any fps entry into service. P&W's shops add capacity after, never instead.

Strain. Zero on Do Nothing in every column. Either widebody item adds $5B for good: the upgrade is -6.48, UltraFan WB -8.02 to -9.00, and both lose before the strain. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, a year after any Re-engine launched now.

Widebody. 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.

Statement: no date anywhere. Our Boeing offer is our Joint Venture share, not a Solo UltraFan, with support before entry into service.

We're pacing that program properly.

other_moves.move: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing and durability work continues inside a flat R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and life-limited part extensions on the installed fleet. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat envelope, not added. This is our answer on the widebody, not a new programme. No widebody programme is launched [RX-0123, RX-0214, RX-0101].

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops: live for the NGSA fleet and sized for a second airframe
other_moves.detail: Partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team. The plan is Rolls-Royce's own. It is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe before that airframe enters service. Our partner's shops add capacity after that and never replace this plan. No dates are disclosed [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Answer to Boeing's engine-sourcing invitation, renewed
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce offers its part of the Joint Venture engine for a future Boeing single-aisle, on standard terms, with no launch discount and no concession. Durability proven before entry into service, as a contract condition. Support and MRO through partner shops in place before entry into service. No dates and no new spend. Rolls-Royce speaks only for its own part [RX-0058, RX-0081, RX-0283].

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms only
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation frame
other_moves.detail: Cash from the Trent and Joint Venture fleets goes first to the balance sheet, then to a 30-40% dividend payout, then to investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0242, RX-0213, RX-0215, RX-0261].

other_moves.move: Rolls-Royce-module durability gates reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round
other_moves.detail: Watson reports the gates with no date: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. Our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service; no pacing bent to any airframer's ramp; no concession to P&W or any airframer. P&W's GTF hot-and-sandy time-on-wing record is the watch item. If a gate fails, the block waits and we tell Airbus and P&W early [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476, R-0970].

other_moves.move: Widebody watch for 2050
other_moves.detail: If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, the ExCo brings one row, A350 first, on the 2050 grid with its item value, worst column against its own bill and the $5B strain shown. Bars (team doctrine, inference): the upgrade needs at least +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB needs a Re-engine on the record and at least +$4B weighted before the strain, so its shortfall sits inside the $1B sub-cap, and must not lose more than its $4B bill in any plausible column. Otherwise the core is protected through time on wing.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields. ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw hold, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold. None of these is a Board item. It is my proposal, both memos recommend it, and nothing struck it.

THE QUESTION, IN CASH AND QUALITY OF EARNINGS [RX-0054]. We made the narrowbody bet, paid for it, and it is earning. The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our narrowbody share is 25.1% in 2045 and 23.3% from 2047: 872 engines this year, 876 a year after that. Narrowbody development money ended at $5.71B, all booked in 2035: our $4B share plus a $1.71B write-off. Today's ΔPV is +9.61 (engine value +15.32, R&D -4.00, write-off -1.71). Following Watson's caution, I credit the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules being in service by any year. This round is about protecting those earnings and the widebody franchise, not adding activity.

GRID, COLUMN BY COLUMN. Item value is the row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'.
- Hold row 'UltraFan NB: hold': +9.61 / +9.62 / +9.61 / +9.86 (S1-S4). Best in every column. Worst column +9.61.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade': row +3.13 / +3.14 / +3.13 / +3.40. Item -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.48 / -6.46. With the $5B strain added back, -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.48 / -1.46. Worst column -6.48 against its own $2B bill. Widebody would go from 55.2% to 60.0% in 2050, but 55.2% already clears the line. McCabe puts the extra engines at about +$0.52B of PV against a $2B bill.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB': row +0.61 / +0.62 / +1.33 / +1.84. Item -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.28 / -8.02. With the strain added back, -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.28 / -3.02. Worst column -9.00 against its own $4B bill. Widebody stays at 55.2% in every column, because it would be ready in 2051, a year after any Re-engine launched now.
- The two widebody items are exclusive, so there is no joint row. Both narrowbody fields are hold only.

WEIGHTS. There is no selection to weigh. The columns are rivals' moves, so P is 0.1 for 'nothing on the record' (inference). Sets (calculation in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-sd/work/r3_decide_calc.py):
- B, the Board's illustrative set, confirmed by McCabe: 0.70 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05. Hold +9.624; upgrade item -6.479 (-1.479 before strain); UltraFan WB item -8.879 (-3.879).
- C/M, my read and McCabe's: 0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05. Same votes; hold +9.623.
- U, uniform: hold +9.675; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
- R, Re-engine-heavy: 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.25. Hold +9.674; upgrade -6.475; UltraFan WB -8.575.
No set changes any vote. Both widebody items lose in every column, even before the strain.

TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing declined a 787 Re-engine. That fails UltraFan WB outright.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: the upgrade fails on the business model (it loses before the strain, and the strain is anti-synergy). UltraFan WB fails on the market and the business model.
- Profitable or not at all [RX-0058]: neither item clears zero.
- Premium cap: the upgrade shortfall (about $6.5B) is more than double the $3B cap. UltraFan WB's ($8.6-8.9B) is far over the $1B sub-cap.
- Reasonable worst case: both items lose more than their own bill in every column.
- Widebody franchise [R-1574]: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 on every held row. The 2.8 pp step in 2042 is the GEnx upgrade. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: Do Nothing commits no new programme money. For the record, capex for either item would be about $0.67B a year (£0.49-0.50bn), plus $5B of strain (about £3.7bn), roughly a year of FY2026 free cash flow guidance.
- My pull toward the 787 ('Why not?' [RX-0117], 'regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]) is real. The grid says why not. The answer is time on wing, not a programme weighed down by a $5B strain.

VETO CHECKS.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature, binding, on t1000_upgrade launch and ultrafan_wb launch. Neither is ordered, so nothing needs revising. Her balance-sheet vetoes are not triggered: no equity, no borrowing, no change in leverage. A fall in the brief's ΔPV is not a trigger.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto on the proposed orders. Maturity is not compressed: the Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2. His conditional veto covers the final statement, the other moves and this rationale. I have written them to his tests: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block or Rolls-Royce content anywhere; nothing that counts on our modules entering service by a year or being on the fps at its EIS; partner shops are ours, with P&W's shops adding capacity only after, never instead; the Boeing answer is Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan, with support in place before entry into service; no fps or Re-engine dates go public.

RED-LINE FLAGS.
- McCabe flagged that an ultrafan_wb launch would break the company rule of no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it. Struck: not ordered.
- The upgrade breaks no overlap red line on the board, since no UltraFan is in development. It is struck on money grounds alone.
- No cancel is available, and nothing orphaned stands: the Joint Venture flies on NGSA [RX-0051].
- overrides is empty.

OBJECTIVES, PLAINLY.
- Narrowbody entry: met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Widebody dominance: met (55.2% at the low point, 5.2 pp above the line).
- Bounded narrowbody risk (at most $4B): not met, locked at $5.71B (the Solo's 2030-2035 spend, folded into the Joint Venture). No order this round moves it. We accepted that because an airframe selected us.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0 strain, and kept only by holding both widebody items. I will not trade it for a widebody programme that pays on no column.

ROUND-2 BOARD ITEMS: closed or carried; see board_response.

DOCTRINE, NOT RECORD. The column weights, the 2050 widebody bars (upgrade +$3B before the strain in every plausible column; UltraFan WB a Re-engine on the record and +$4B weighted before the strain) and the worst-case rule are team doctrine (inference). On the UltraFan WB bar I take McCabe's +$4B over the Board's +$3B: only +$4B keeps the shortfall inside the Board's own $1B sub-cap.

"We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically." [RX-0058]

memo_weighing.cfo: Weighed heavily, and adopted in full. McCabe confirms weights B as the base and gives her own set M (my set C). Her numbers match mine: hold is +9.624 on B, +9.675 uniform; the upgrade is -6.48 on any weights; UltraFan WB is -8.88 on B and -8.58 on U/R. She withholds her co-signature, binding, on both widebody launches. Neither is ordered, so there is nothing to revise. She confirms no new programme money and that narrowbody spend ended at $5.71B, with the Joint Venture saving about £1.7bn against the Solo, as she said in 2035. She confirms the capital frame and that no balance-sheet trigger is in play. On S2 she shows there is nothing to concede (+$0.01B, about £7m). I take her 2050 bar for UltraFan WB (+$4B weighted before the strain) over the Board's +$3B, because only hers keeps the shortfall inside the $1B sub-cap. Her flag that an UltraFan WB launch would break the no-programme-to-fly-it rule is noted and struck, since it is not ordered.
memo_weighing.ops: Weighed heavily on readiness, support and statement discipline, and adopted in full. Watson concurs with Do Nothing and invokes no Civil veto on the orders. The Joint Venture engine took P&W's full six years for GTF2, not compressed, and is in service on NGSA with no fleet event on the record. P&W's GTF time on wing in hot and sandy conditions is our watch item, and our module proof covers hot and harsh conditions. I wrote the statement, the other moves and the rationale to his conditional veto: no date, year or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block; nothing that counts on our modules being in service by a year or on the fps at its EIS; partner shops ours, P&W's adding capacity after, never instead; the Boeing answer is our part of the Joint Venture engine, not a Solo UltraFan. I kept the fps planning gates internal. His capacity read (narrowbody load at 84% of what we sized for in round 2) is advice and holds. His view that the upgrade would compete for the same engineers as our module proof supports the hold.

decision.predictions:
2045 round, private:
- Boeing launches the fps: about 0.40. If it does, the 10-year variant is likelier (it promised headroom), and code 7 is likelier than code 5, as its sourcing plan says. S2 exactly (10-year, code 5): about 0.05-0.15. Either way about +$0.01B to us, because a late entry into service barely counts by 2056.
- 787 Re-engine: about 0.10 (Boeing called the 787 'the most efficient airplane in its class' and is adding Charleston capacity).
- A350 Re-engine as well: about 0.05 (Airbus's widebody focus is the A350 family and the A350F).
- CFM/GE: an Open Fan launch from RISE is unlikely, about 0.10 ('when an aircraft needs it'). If launched, it is ready no earlier than 2055, off our grid. No further GEnx move expected this round.
